::: {.callout-note title="Sources"}
**CLRS** ch. 2 (counting inversions — a pair count), ch. 10 (direct addressing) and appendix A (manipulating summations) · **CPH** ch. 1 (running-time estimates) and ch. 22 (combinatorics: binomial coefficients, inclusion–exclusion) · **CP-Algorithms**: Inclusion–exclusion principle · Coverage: the contribution swap over subarrays, subsequences and pairs; cover counts $(i+1)(n-i)$; winner spans; sums over pairs by algebra, sorting and bits; pair counting by sweep and histogram; index-and-value conditions; counting windows with a property; complementary counting and inclusion–exclusion; fixing the middle of a triple; value-indexed tables.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="What you will be able to do"}
- Replace a double loop over windows by a **dot product with cover counts**: slot $i$ lies in $(i+1)(n-i)$ subarrays, so any $\sum_{\text{windows}} \text{linear}(\text{window})$ is one pass (@sec-cnt-a1).
- Count the subarrays in which an element is the **maximum** (or minimum) with monotonic-stack spans and opposite tie-breaking, and hence evaluate $\sum (\max - \min)$ in $O(n)$ (@sec-cnt-a2).
- Evaluate a **sum over all pairs** — of products, absolute differences, XORs or Hamming distances — in $O(n)$ or $O(n \log n)$ by algebra, by sorting with rank weights $2k - n + 1$, or bit by bit with $c(n-c)$ (@sec-cnt-pairsum).
- Count **pairs** by fixing the right end and charging `seen[value]`, or by closing a histogram with $\binom{c}{2}$ — including complementary bucket counts modulo $k$ (@sec-cnt-a3) — and separate a condition that mixes **indices and values** into keys (@sec-cnt-idxval).
- Count subarrays **with a property** by prefix-hash equality or by $\text{atMost}(K) - \text{atMost}(K-1)$, say which survives negative numbers (@sec-cnt-a4), and count the **complement** instead when "bad" is easier to describe, with inclusion–exclusion when two bad events overlap (@sec-cnt-comp).
- Count **triples** by fixing the middle: multiply left and right counts when the outer indices are unrelated, query a value interval when they are, and recognise when small values make the value itself an index (@sec-cnt-a5).
:::

## Why this matters {#sec-cnt-why}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
The earlier chapters of this volume taught you to *read* an array: sweep it, sort it, index it, wrap a structure around it. This chapter is about the questions where the array is not the input but the **index of the answer** — "sum over all subarrays", "how many pairs satisfy $P$", "count the triples with $a \le |x-y| \le b$". The naive answer is always the same: two or three nested loops, $O(n^2)$ or $O(n^3)$ windows, and at $n = 10^5$ that is $5 \cdot 10^9$ windows and you are done as a candidate. The technique that fixes it is one move, made three ways. **Re-index the sum.** Instead of walking the windows and adding up what is inside them, walk the *elements* and ask each how many windows it is inside: slot $i$ of an $n$-cell array is covered by $(i+1)(n-i)$ subarrays, so $\sum_{\text{subarrays}} \text{sum} = \sum_i a_i (i+1)(n-i)$ — a dot product, one pass, and the whole of @sec-cnt-p1-oddsum. When the window statistic is not linear (a maximum, a $\max - \min$) the same swap still works but the cover count becomes geometric: the element is charged with the subarrays in which it *rules*, which is a product of two monotonic-stack spans (@sec-cnt-a2). When the object is a pair rather than a window, the same swap sums over pairs by sorting or by bits (@sec-cnt-pairsum), and to *count* pairs you fix one end and let a histogram answer for the other (@sec-cnt-a3). When the object is a window with a *property*, the answer is either an equality among prefix values (@sec-cnt-a4) or a difference of two easier counts — "exactly $K$" is "at most $K$" minus "at most $K-1$" — and when the bad windows are easier to describe than the good ones, you count everything and subtract (@sec-cnt-comp). And when the object is a triple, one of its three indices usually appears in two of the three conditions: **fix the middle**, and the two remaining conditions become an interval query over values, answered by a histogram of a small range (@sec-cnt-a5).
:::

This chapter opens Part IV, and it stands on tools you already own. The prefix-sum identity $P[j] - P[i]$ of @sec-pref-def and its hash-map counting form @sec-pref-hash (with the prefix XOR of @sec-pref-other) turn "a window with a property" into "a pair of prefixes". The complement lookups and grouping keys of @sec-hash are how pairs are counted in one pass. The two-pointer counting of @sec-tp ("for each right end, how many left ends") and the window counting of @sec-sw-a4 ("everything ending at $r$", and "at most $K$ minus at most $K-1$") count pairs and windows when the array is sorted or non-negative. The value-as-index tables of @sec-lts-a5 and @sec-idx, the "fix two rows" reduction of @sec-mat, and the frequency-table designs of @sec-ds round out the toolkit. What this chapter adds is the *reframing* — the decision of which object to iterate over — and the arithmetic that makes the reframing exact.

The lessons build that reframing in eight steps:

- **A1 — the contribution swap.** $\sum_{\text{windows}} \to \sum_{\text{elements}} \times \text{cover count}$, proved by swapping the order of summation, with the cover count $(i+1)(n-i)$ derived by counting start and end choices.
- **A2 — spans: who does a window belong to.** When the statistic is a maximum, credit each window to its winner; a monotonic stack measures the spans, and opposite tie-breaking stops equal values being charged twice.
- **A3 — sums over all pairs.** The same swap with pairs instead of windows: algebra for products, rank weights after sorting for $|a_i - a_j|$, and one column per bit for XOR.
- **A4 — counting pairs.** Fix the right end and charge `seen[complement]`; or close each group with $\binom{c}{2}$.
- **A5 — index and value conditions.** Separate a condition like $j - i = a_i + a_j$ into a key per side; use a size bound when it cannot be separated.
- **A6 — windows with a property.** Prefix equality and at-most differences, with a clear account of which needs non-negative entries.
- **A7 — complementary counting.** Count everything, subtract the bad; inclusion–exclusion when two bad events overlap.
- **A8 — triples and small values.** Fix the middle; multiply left and right counts, or query a value interval; let the value be the address when the range is tiny.

Part B turns each lesson into a pattern with at least two fully solved problems. The next chapter (GCD and number-theoretic arrays) keeps the counting mindset and adds divisibility: counting pairs by their GCD, and harmonic loops over multiples like the one in @sec-cnt-pidx-pleasant.

## Part A — Lessons

## A1. The contribution swap {#sec-cnt-a1}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
You are asked for the sum of something over all subarrays. There are $\binom{n+1}{2}$ of them, so the loop is $O(n^2)$ and at $n = 10^5$ it is hopeless — unless the quantity you are adding is **linear in the elements**, in which case you never needed the windows at all. Swap the order of summation: an element $a_i$ is added once for every subarray that contains it, and those subarrays are exactly the choices of a start in $0..i$ and an end in $i..n-1$, i.e. $(i+1)(n-i)$ of them. So $\sum_{\text{subarrays}} \text{sum}(\text{subarray}) = \sum_i a_i (i+1)(n-i)$. Two "which one do I iterate over" questions with the same answer but wildly different cost — and the cheaper one is always "iterate over the things that are fewest", here the $n$ elements rather than the $n^2$ windows.
:::

The counting is worth doing slowly once, because every later variant reuses it. A subarray is a pair $(\text{start}, \text{end})$ with $\text{start} \le i \le \text{end}$. Fix $i$. The start may be any of $0, 1, \dots, i$ — that is $i+1$ choices; the end may be any of $i, i+1, \dots, n-1$ — that is $n-i$ choices. The two choices are independent, so the number of windows containing slot $i$ is the product $(i+1)(n-i)$. For $n = 4$ the cover counts are $[4, 6, 6, 4]$: the two middle slots are covered half again as often as the two ends, which is the shape you would guess from the picture — a cell in the middle sits inside more windows — and the shape a `for start: for end:` loop produces if you instrument it.

Written as algebra, the whole technique is one exchange of two finite sums. A subarray is a pair $(l, r)$ with $0 \le l \le r \le n-1$, and its sum is $\sum_{i=l}^{r} a_i$. Sum over all subarrays, then exchange the order — the double sum runs over the triples $(l, i, r)$ with $l \le i \le r$, and they can be listed by $i$ first:

$$\sum_{l=0}^{n-1}\sum_{r=l}^{n-1}\sum_{i=l}^{r} a_i \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i \cdot \#\{(l, r) : 0 \le l \le i \le r \le n-1\} \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i\,(i+1)(n-i).$$ {#eq-cnt-swap}

Nothing in @eq-cnt-swap is specific to sums of windows. Whenever an answer is $\sum_{\text{objects}} \sum_{\text{elements in the object}} w(\text{element})$, exchanging the sums gives $\sum_{\text{elements}} w(\text{element}) \cdot \#\{\text{objects containing it}\}$, and the work moves to counting that set. For subsequences instead of subarrays the set is "all subsets of the other $n - 1$ elements", so each element lies in $2^{n-1}$ subsequences and the sum over all subsequence sums is $2^{n-1} \sum_i a_i$; for pairs it is "the other $n-1$ elements", which gives $\sum_{i<j}(a_i + a_j) = (n-1)\sum_i a_i$. @fig-cnt-a1-contain shows the set for subarrays: it is a rectangle of start choices times end choices.

::: {#fig-cnt-a1-contain}

```{python}
#| echo: false

a1c_cells = [[(f"[{l}..{r}]" if l <= r else "") for r in range(a1c_n)] for l in range(a1c_n)]

            pointers=[(a1c_i, "slot i = 2", "amber", "top")], cell_w=1.2)
```

All $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ subarrays of a length-5 array, placed by start (row) and end (column); the empty lower triangle is "end before start". The cyan block is every subarray that contains slot $2$: start in $\{0, 1, 2\}$ and end in $\{2, 3, 4\}$, a $3 \times 3$ rectangle — $(i+1)(n-i) = 9$ windows. Move the slot and the rectangle changes shape but stays a rectangle, which is why the count is a product.

:::

```{python}
def cover_counts(n):
    return [(i + 1) * (n - i) for i in range(n)]


def all_subarrays(a):
    return [a[j:k + 1] for j in range(len(a)) for k in range(j, len(a))]


a = [2, 3, 5, 7]
w = cover_counts(len(a))
assert w == [4, 6, 6, 4]
assert sum(w) == 4 * 5 * 6 // 6 == 20          # sum_i (i+1)(n-i) = n(n+1)(n+2)/6
assert len(all_subarrays(a)) == 4 * 5 // 2 == 10
assert sum(sum(s) for s in all_subarrays(a)) == sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, w)) == 84

# the same swap restricted to odd-length windows
def a1_odd_cover(n):
    return [((i + 1) * (n - i) + 1) // 2 for i in range(n)]


assert a1_odd_cover(4) == [2, 3, 3, 2]
assert sum(a1_odd_cover(4)) == 10              # = sum of the ODD window lengths, not their count
assert sum(k - j + 1 for j in range(4) for k in range(j, 4)
           if (k - j + 1) % 2 == 1) == 10
oddsum = sum(sum(s) for s in all_subarrays(a) if len(s) % 2 == 1)
assert oddsum == sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, a1_odd_cover(4))) == 42
for n in range(1, 31):                         # cross-check both identities
    arr = [random.randint(1, 50) for _ in range(n)]
    cov = cover_counts(n)
    assert sum(sum(s) for s in all_subarrays(arr)) == sum(x * y for x, y in zip(arr, cov))
    oc = a1_odd_cover(n)
    assert sum(sum(s) for s in all_subarrays(arr) if len(s) % 2) == sum(
        x * y for x, y in zip(arr, oc))
    # the cover count is exactly the number of (l, r) with l <= i <= r
    assert all(sum(1 for l in range(n) for r in range(l, n) if l <= i <= r) == cov[i]
               for i in range(n))
# the same exchange for subsequences and for pairs
from itertools import combinations
for n in range(1, 9):
    arr = [random.randint(-5, 9) for _ in range(n)]
    subseq_total = sum(sum(c) for k in range(1, n + 1) for c in combinations(arr, k))
    assert subseq_total == 2 ** (n - 1) * sum(arr)
    assert sum(x + y for x, y in combinations(arr, 2)) == (n - 1) * sum(arr)
```

```{python}
                   ["#ends (n-i)",      "4", "3", "2", "1"],
                   ["(i+1)(n-i)",       "4", "6", "6", "4"],
                   ["a[i] * cover",     "8", "18", "30", "28"]],
```

Rows 3 and 4 are the two independent choices, recorded as counts: $i+1$ starts (`1, 2, 3, 4`) and $n-i$ ends (`4, 3, 2, 1`), so at $i = 0$ there is one start but four ends, and at $i = 3$ four starts but one end. Row 5 is their product, row 6 the element's credit, and $8 + 18 + 30 + 28 = 84$ is the sum over all ten subarrays — obtained without ever naming a subarray.

:::

Two cautions, both of which recur all chapter. **(1) The swap needs linearity.** $\sum_{\text{windows}} \text{sum}(\text{window})$ rearranges because addition is associative and commutative; $\sum_{\text{windows}} \max(\text{window})$ does *not* rearrange this way, and trying to force it is how people write wrong $O(n)$ solutions to @sec-cnt-p1-ranges. What you can do with a maximum is change the *domain* of the credit from "windows containing $i$" to "windows in which $i$ is the winner" — that is @sec-cnt-a2. **(2) A cover count is not a window count.** $\sum_i (i+1)(n-i) = \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6} = 20$ for $n = 4$, while there are only $\binom{n+1}{2} = 10$ windows: the cover sum counts *windows weighted by length*. That is a legitimate quantity (it is the sum of lengths) but it is not a check on your arithmetic, and the odd-length version bites harder — $\sum_i \lceil (i+1)(n-i)/2 \rceil = 10$ at $n = 4$ is the sum of odd window lengths, whereas the *number* of odd-length windows is $6$.

The number of odd-length windows is a pleasant one-liner and it is worth deriving rather than memorising, because the derivation is the same trick this chapter keeps using. Write a window as a pair of **cut points** $(j, k+1)$ with $0 \le j < k+1 \le n$; the length is $k - j + 1$, so the window has odd length exactly when the two cuts have *different* parity. Among $0 .. n$ there are $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1$ even cuts and $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ odd ones, so odd windows $= (\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1)\lceil n/2 \rceil$ and even windows are the same-parity pairs $\binom{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1}{2} + \binom{\lceil n/2 \rceil}{2}$. At $n = 4$: even cuts $\{0,2,4\}$, odd cuts $\{1,3\}$, so $3 \times 2 = 6$ odd and $3 + 1 = 4$ even — totalling $\binom{5}{2} = 10$. Parity is a bucket, and counting is multiplication: @sec-cnt-a3 in miniature.

## A2. Spans: who does a window belong to {#sec-cnt-a2}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
"Sum of $\max$ over all subarrays" looks linear-friendly but is not: a maximum is not a sum of per-element contributions. The repair is to keep the swap and change what is being counted. Ask instead: for each slot $i$, **in how many subarrays is $a_i$ the maximum?** If the answer is $\text{left}_i \times \text{right}_i$ — how far left the boundary may sit, how far right — then the credit $\sum_i a_i \cdot \text{left}_i \cdot \text{right}_i$ is exactly the quantity you wanted. Both spans are the "distance to the nearest element that blocks me" that a monotonic stack hands you in $O(n)$; @sec-cx-p3-temperatures is the book's other use of the same one-pass stack (there the question is "how long until a warmer day"), and the counting form is developed from scratch in @sec-cnt-p1-ranges because you do not need the stack to be a topic yet.
:::

Left span for slot $i$ = the number of choices of the window's start = the distance to the previous element **strictly greater** than $a_i$, or to the left edge if there is none. Right span = the number of choices of the end = the distance to the next element **greater than or equal to** $a_i$, or to the right edge. Multiply, weight by $a_i$, sum. Then the subtlety that decides whether the code is right:

**Ties must be broken in opposite directions on the two sides.** With duplicates there is no unique maximum, so the algorithm must *appoint* one — and the appointment must cover every window exactly once. The rule that works is "pop while $\le$ when scanning left-to-right, pop while $<$ when scanning right-to-left" (or the exact mirror image). The left pass pops equal values, so a slot's left span reaches *past* its equals; the right pass stops at an equal value, so a window whose maximum appears twice is credited to the **rightmost** of them. Every window therefore gets exactly one winner. Mirror both comparisons and the winner becomes the leftmost — also correct; keep the same strictness on both sides and the appointment breaks. Take $[3, 3]$: with opposite tie-breaking the two slots are credited $[1, 2]$ windows — three claims for the three windows $[3], [3], [3,3]$, and the maximum credit is $3 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot 2 = 9$, which is right. Use the **same pop predicate as on the left** — both passes pop equals — and the credits become $[2, 2]$ on $[3, 3]$: four claims for three windows, and the sum of maxima comes out $12$ against a true $9$. On $[1, 3, 3]$ the same slip reports $22$ where the truth is $16$; flip the slip to "strict on both sides" and the credits shrink to $[1, 2, 1]$ — only $4$ claims for $6$ windows — and the answer drifts the other way to $10$, which is the failure mode @sec-cnt-p1-ranges warns about in its edge list.

```{python}
def a2_spans(nums, greater):
    """left[i], right[i]: how far slot i rules as max (greater=True) or min.

    Ties are broken in opposite directions: pop while <= going left, < going right.
    """
    n = len(nums)
    left, right, st = [0] * n, [0] * n, []
    for i, v in enumerate(nums):
        while st and (nums[st[-1]] <= v if greater else nums[st[-1]] >= v):
            st.pop()
        left[i] = i - st[-1] if st else i + 1
        st.append(i)
    st = []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        v = nums[i]
        while st and (nums[st[-1]] < v if greater else nums[st[-1]] > v):
            st.pop()
        right[i] = st[-1] - i if st else n - i
        st.append(i)
    return left, right


L, R = a2_spans([1, 3, 3], True)
assert (L, R) == ([1, 2, 3], [1, 1, 1]) and [l * r for l, r in zip(L, R)] == [1, 2, 3]
M, N = a2_spans([1, 3, 3], False)
assert (M, N) == ([1, 1, 2], [3, 1, 1]) and [l * r for l, r in zip(M, N)] == [3, 1, 2]
assert sum(v * l * r for v, l, r in zip([1, 3, 3], L, R)) == 16     # sum of maxes
assert sum(v * l * r for v, l, r in zip([1, 3, 3], M, N)) == 12     # sum of mins
assert 16 - 12 == 4                                                 # sum of ranges

for trial in range(120):
    arr = [random.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 9))]
    ss = [arr[j:k + 1] for j in range(len(arr)) for k in range(j, len(arr))]
    La, Ra = a2_spans(arr, True)
    Mb, Nb = a2_spans(arr, False)
    assert sum(max(s) for s in ss) == sum(v * l * r for v, l, r in zip(arr, La, Ra))
    assert sum(min(s) for s in ss) == sum(v * l * r for v, l, r in zip(arr, Mb, Nb))
    assert sum(max(s) - min(s) for s in ss) == sum(
        v * (l * r - x * y) for v, l, r, x, y in zip(arr, La, Ra, Mb, Nb))
```

```{python}
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["index i",          "0", "1", "2"],
                   ["nums[i]",          "1", "3", "3"],
                   ["max: left span",   "1", "2", "3"],
                   ["max: right span",  "1", "1", "1"],
                   ["max credit L*R",   "1", "2", "3"],
                   ["min credit L*R",   "3", "1", "2"]],
```

The two cyan cells are the tie: the run of `3`s is credited by the opposite-comparison rule to its rightmost member, so slot 2 takes $[3,3]$ as well as its own single-cell window. Both credit rows add to $6 = \binom{4}{2}$ — every window appoints exactly one maximum slot and exactly one minimum slot (the amber cell says slot $0$ is the minimum of the three windows that start at it), which is the certificate that the tie rule is doing its job. Sum of maxima $= 1\cdot1 + 3\cdot2 + 3\cdot3 = 16$, sum of minima $= 1\cdot3 + 3\cdot1 + 3\cdot2 = 12$, so the sum of ranges is $4$ — and the six per-window ranges $[0, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0]$ add up to the same $4$.

:::

Three things to take from the cell. Distances are not credits: `a2_spans` returns **distances to the blocking element**, and the number of windows is the product of the two distances, not their sum. Sum of $\max$ and sum of $\min$ use the *same* code with `greater` flipped, and the difference of the two credits is the sum of ranges — $\sum (\max - \min) = \sum \max - \sum \min$ is linearity of a different kind, applied at the level of the statistic rather than the element. And "sum over windows" problems whose statistic is an extremum are nearly always this: **one extremal role, one stack, one credit** — so a problem that asks for $\max + \min$, or $\max^2$, or "count windows where the max is unique" is the same machinery with a different weight. The full ladder, including the $O(n^2)$ version you should write first to have an oracle, is @sec-cnt-p1-ranges. The monotonic stack itself — and the classic "sum of subarray minimums" (LC 907, the min half of this computation, usually asked with a modulus) — belongs to the stack volume of the book; here the stack is used only as a tool that measures spans, and the counting argument is the part to keep.

## A3. Sums over all pairs {#sec-cnt-pairsum}

**From windows to pairs.** A1 and A2 summed over the $\binom{n+1}{2}$ windows; the other quadratic family in a statement is the $\binom{n}{2}$ **pairs** $i < j$. The swap is the same — ask what each element contributes — but a pair has two members, so the contribution of $a_i$ depends on *who it is paired with*, and the work is in organising the partners so that their effect can be added up in one step.

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
"Sum of $f(a_i, a_j)$ over all pairs" has three standard escapes from the double loop. **Algebra** when $f$ splits: $\sum_{i<j}(a_i + a_j)$ gives every element $n - 1$ partners, and $\sum_{i<j} a_i a_j$ is half of $(\sum a)^2 - \sum a^2$. **Sorting** when $f$ is a distance: after sorting, $|a_i - a_j|$ is just "later minus earlier", so the element of rank $k$ is added $k$ times and subtracted $n - 1 - k$ times. **Bits** when $f$ is bitwise: XOR, AND and OR act on each bit separately, so count the ones in each bit column and multiply. In every case the pair loop disappears into a count.
:::

The sorting case is the one to prove carefully, because it is the one interviewers ask for. Sort the values into $b_0 \le b_1 \le \cdots \le b_{n-1}$; the set of pairs is unchanged, so the sum is unchanged. For $k < m$ we have $|b_m - b_k| = b_m - b_k$, so

$$\sum_{k<m} |b_m - b_k| \;=\; \sum_{m} b_m \cdot \#\{k : k < m\} \;-\; \sum_{k} b_k \cdot \#\{m : m > k\} \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} b_k\,\bigl(k - (n-1-k)\bigr) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} b_k\,(2k - n + 1).$$ {#eq-cnt-rank}

The same total arrives as a running sweep: when the cursor reaches $b_m$, the $m$ earlier values are each subtracted once, so the step adds $m \cdot b_m - P_m$, where $P_m$ is the sum of the earlier values. That **count-and-sum of the earlier ones** is the general tool whenever the charge of a pair is linear in the earlier member; @sec-cnt-p4-xortri uses it with indices in place of values. For bitwise $f$ the exchange is over bits: in bit $b$, $c_b$ numbers have a `1`; a pair's XOR has that bit exactly when the pair takes one `1` and one `0`, which happens for $c_b(n - c_b)$ pairs, so $\sum_{i<j} (a_i \oplus a_j) = \sum_b 2^b\, c_b (n - c_b)$. AND needs both ones, $\binom{c_b}{2}$; OR needs *not both zeros*, $\binom{n}{2} - \binom{n - c_b}{2}$ — complementary counting (@sec-cnt-comp) inside one bit.

```{python}
def pairsum_brute(a, f):
    return sum(f(a[i], a[j]) for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a)))


def pairsum_absdiff(a):
    b = sorted(a)
    n = len(b)
    return sum(x * (2 * k - n + 1) for k, x in enumerate(b))       # (eq-cnt-rank)


def pairsum_absdiff_sweep(a):
    total = prefix = 0
    for m, x in enumerate(sorted(a)):
        total += m * x - prefix              # x minus each of the m earlier values
        prefix += x
    return total


def pairsum_products(a):
    s = sum(a)
    return (s * s - sum(x * x for x in a)) // 2


def pairsum_bits(a, op, bits=20):
    n, total = len(a), 0
    for b in range(bits):
        c = sum((x >> b) & 1 for x in a)
        if op == "xor":
            pairs = c * (n - c)
        elif op == "and":
            pairs = c * (c - 1) // 2
        else:                                                    # "or": not both zero
            pairs = n * (n - 1) // 2 - (n - c) * (n - c - 1) // 2
        total += pairs << b
    return total


assert pairsum_absdiff([8, 1, 4, 3]) == pairsum_absdiff_sweep([8, 1, 4, 3]) == 22
assert [2 * k - 4 + 1 for k in range(4)] == [-3, -1, 1, 3]
for _ in range(200):
    arr = [random.randint(-30, 30) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))]
    assert pairsum_absdiff(arr) == pairsum_absdiff_sweep(arr) == pairsum_brute(arr, lambda x, y: abs(x - y))
    assert pairsum_products(arr) == pairsum_brute(arr, lambda x, y: x * y)
    nat = [abs(x) * 997 % (1 << 12) for x in arr]
    assert pairsum_bits(nat, "xor") == pairsum_brute(nat, lambda x, y: x ^ y)
    assert pairsum_bits(nat, "and") == pairsum_brute(nat, lambda x, y: x & y)
    assert pairsum_bits(nat, "or") == pairsum_brute(nat, lambda x, y: x | y)
# index differences are a sum over pairs too: sum_{i<j} (j - i) = C(n+1, 3)
assert all(pairsum_brute(list(range(n)), lambda x, y: y - x) == math.comb(n + 1, 3)
           for n in range(1, 12))
```

::: {#fig-cnt-pairsum}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
ps_b = sorted([8, 1, 4, 3])
ps_w = [2 * k - len(ps_b) + 1 for k in range(len(ps_b))]
ps_c = [x * w for x, w in zip(ps_b, ps_w)]
assert sum(ps_c) == 22 == pairsum_absdiff([8, 1, 4, 3])


def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["rank k", "0", "1", "2", "3"],
                   ["sorted value", *map(str, ps_b)],
                   ["added (k times)", "0", "1", "2", "3"],
                   ["subtracted (n-1-k)", "3", "2", "1", "0"],
                   ["weight 2k-n+1", *map(str, ps_w)],
                   ["contribution", *map(str, ps_c)]],
           colors={(4, 0 + 1): "pink", (4, 4): "green", (5, 4): "green", (5, 1): "pink"},
           cell_w=1.1)
V.show(draw)
```

`[8, 1, 4, 3]` sorted. The smallest value is subtracted in all three of its pairs (weight $-3$), the largest is added in all three (weight $+3$), and the middle ranks partly cancel. The contributions add to $22 = 2 + 3 + 7 + 1 + 5 + 4$, the six pairwise distances.

:::

Two warnings travel with these formulas. A sum over pairs grows like $n^2$ times the values, so it overflows 32 bits long before the pair *count* does — @sec-cnt-psum-weird's answer reaches about $10^{14}$. And the rank weight needs the list sorted: on the unsorted `[8, 1, 4, 3]` the same weights give $-3 \cdot 8 - 1 + 4 + 9 = -12$, a negative "sum of distances".

## A4. Counting pairs: fix one end, or close a histogram {#sec-cnt-a3}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A pair is a window of two positions, so the same re-indexing applies with $O(n^2)$ pairs replaced by $n$ decisions. Two shapes. **Fix the right end**: sweep $j$ from left to right holding a count of everything seen, and when you arrive at $j$ add how many earlier indices are compatible with it — for equal-value pairs, `ans += seen[v]; seen[v] += 1`. **Or don't sweep at all**: count the histogram first, and note that a group of $c$ mutually-compatible items contributes $\binom{c}{2}$ pairs. Both are $O(n)$; the first is what you need when the compatibility relation is *asymmetric* or you must respect index order, the second when it is an equivalence relation and order is irrelevant.
:::

Read the charges position by position and the two forms become the same arithmetic. At index $2$ the value `1` already has two earlier friends, so the sweep adds $2$; at index $4$ the value `2` has one, so it adds $1$. The group of `1`s therefore accumulates $0 + 1 + 2 = 3$ pairs and the group of `2`s $0 + 1 = 1$, totalling $4$ — which is $\binom{3}{2} + \binom{2}{2} = 3 + 1$, the histogram form arriving at the same number by a different route. The sweep charges each pair to its **right** member, the histogram charges each pair to its **group**. Choosing between them is choosing which loop you want to avoid.

```{python}
def pairs_equal_scan(a):
    seen, ans = Counter(), 0
    for v in a:
        ans += seen[v]              # pair (earlier i, here): charge to the right end
        seen[v] += 1
    return ans


def pairs_equal_hist(a):
    return sum(c * (c - 1) // 2 for c in Counter(a).values())


def pairs_target_scan(a, t):
    seen, ans = Counter(), 0
    for v in a:
        ans += seen[t - v]          # the complement is looked up, not searched
        seen[v] += 1
    return ans


assert pairs_equal_scan([1, 1, 1, 2, 2]) == pairs_equal_hist([1, 1, 1, 2, 2]) == 4
assert pairs_equal_scan([1, 2, 3]) == 0
assert pairs_target_scan([1, 5, 7, 3, 6], 8) == 2        # (1,7) and (5,3)
assert pairs_target_scan([1, 5, 3, 6], 8) == 1           # 7 is absent, so only (5,3)
assert pairs_target_scan([1, 1, 1], 2) == 3              # a value may be its own complement
assert math.comb(3, 2) + math.comb(2, 2) == 4
# index-order-sensitive relations break the histogram form
a = [3, 1, 2, 1]
s = 0
for i in range(len(a)):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(a)):
        if a[i] > a[j]:
            s += 1
assert s == 4                       # (3,1), (3,2), (3,1) and (2,1)
assert sum(c * (c - 1) // 2 for c in Counter(a).values()) == 1   # the two 1s only
# the per-position charges drawn in the figure
seen, a3_charges, total = Counter(), [], 0
for v in [1, 1, 1, 2, 2]:
    a3_charges.append(seen[v])
    total += seen[v]
    seen[v] += 1
assert a3_charges == [0, 1, 2, 0, 1] and total == 4
```

::: {#fig-cnt-a3}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["index",                "0", "1", "2", "3", "4"],
                   ["a[i]",                 "1", "1", "1", "2", "2"],
                   ["earlier equals",       "0", "1", "2", "0", "1"],
                   ["charge to right end",  "0", "1", "2", "0", "1"],
                   ["running total",        "0", "1", "3", "3", "4"]],
           colors={(3, 3): "cyan", (3, 5): "amber", (4, 5): "green",
                   (2, 1): "muted", (2, 4): "muted"},
           cell_w=1.1)
V.show(draw)
```

Rows 3 and 4 coincide by construction — the charge *is* the number of earlier equals, read before the current element is inserted — and row 5 is their prefix sum, ending at the answer $4$. The two muted cells are where a group restarts: index $3$ is the first `2`, so it pairs with nothing, exactly as index $0$ is the first `1`. Read row 5 as the sweep and the group columns as the histogram and you have both rungs of @sec-cnt-p2-goodpairs in one picture.

:::

The one place the two forms genuinely differ is **index order**. "Pairs with $a_i = a_j$" is symmetric, so a histogram is enough. "Pairs with $i < j$ and $a_i > a_j$" (an inversion, CLRS ch. 2) is not: on `[3, 1, 2, 1]` there are $4$ inversions while the equal-value histogram sees only the pair of `1`s. The sweep form generalises to those (fix the right end, ask a structure how many earlier items are smaller — a Fenwick tree, which is later territory), while $\binom{c}{2}$ does not.

Overflow is a real design decision here rather than a footnote, because pair counts grow quadratically: $\binom{60000}{2} = 1{,}799{,}970{,}000$ fits in a signed 32-bit int with about $16\%$ of headroom and $\binom{10^5}{2} = 4{,}999{,}950{,}000$ does not fit at all (@sec-cnt-p2-goodpairs goes over the same cliff). Accumulate in 64 bits in C++/Java; in Python it is free.

## A5. Index and value conditions {#sec-cnt-idxval}

**From values to positions.** A4's relations looked only at values: $a_i = a_j$, or $a_i + a_j \equiv 0$. Many statements also put the **indices** into the condition — "$a_j - a_i = j - i$", "$j - i = a_i + a_j$", "$a_i \cdot a_j = i + j$", "equal values at distance at least $d$". The index stops being a mere address and becomes part of the data, and the counting tools of A4 apply only after you decide what to do with it.

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Treat the index as a second number that each element carries, and ask whether the condition can be split into "something about $i$" equal to "something about $j$". If it can, compute that something per position and you are back to A4: equal keys on both sides mean a histogram, different keys on the two sides mean a sweep that reads one key and writes the other. If it cannot be split, look for a **bound**: when a product of values must equal a sum of indices, the values involved must be small, and only a few candidates per element survive. And conditions on the *distance* between indices ("at least $d$ apart") are handled by the order of the loop — insert an element into the table only once it is far enough behind the cursor.
:::

There are four recurring shapes, and each has one move:

1. **Separable and symmetric.** $a_j - a_i = j - i \iff a_i - i = a_j - j$: the key $a_i - i$ is computed the same way on both sides, so group by it and add $\binom{c}{2}$. This is CF 1520D, homed in @sec-hash (its card is in @sec-cnt-pidx).
2. **Separable but asymmetric.** $j - i = a_i + a_j \iff i + a_i = j - a_j$: the left member contributes the key $i + a_i$, the right member the key $j - a_j$. A histogram cannot pair two different functions, so fix the right end (@sec-cnt-a3): read `cnt[j - a_j]`, then write `cnt[j + a_j]` — @sec-cnt-pidx-message.
3. **Not separable, but bounded.** $a_i \cdot a_j = i + j$ ties a product to a sum. Since $i + j < 2n$, only pairs with a small product qualify, and for a fixed $i$ the partner must satisfy $j \equiv -i \pmod{a_i}$; stepping through that residue class costs $O(n / a_i)$, and with distinct values the total is a harmonic sum, $O(n \log n)$ — @sec-cnt-pidx-pleasant.
4. **A distance constraint.** "Pairs with $a_i = a_j$ and $j - i \ge d$": when the cursor is at $j$, the eligible partners are exactly the indices $\le j - d$, so insert `a[j - d]` into the table *just before* reading it — a delayed insertion, and the order of the loop enforces the index condition for free.

Index conditions that are inequalities between keys ("$a_i - i < a_j - j$") turn the count into an inversion-like count: sort or use a Fenwick tree (later volume). The point of this lesson is the reflex of rewriting the condition until it says which per-index number to put in the table.

```{python}
def idx_same_diff(a):                                  # shape 1: one key on both sides
    return sum(c * (c - 1) // 2 for c in Counter(v - i for i, v in enumerate(a)).values())


def idx_two_keys(a):                                   # shape 2: j - i = a_i + a_j
    cnt, ans = Counter(), 0
    for j, v in enumerate(a):
        ans += cnt[j - v]                              # read the right-end key
        cnt[j + v] += 1                                # write the left-end key
    return ans


def idx_far_equal(a, d):                               # shape 4: a_i == a_j and j - i >= d
    cnt, ans = Counter(), 0
    for j, v in enumerate(a):
        if j - d >= 0:
            cnt[a[j - d]] += 1                         # a[j-d] just became eligible
        ans += cnt[v]
    return ans


def idx_brute(a, cond):
    return sum(1 for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a)) if cond(i, j))


for _ in range(300):
    a = [random.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 12))]
    d = random.randint(1, 4)
    assert idx_same_diff(a) == idx_brute(a, lambda i, j: a[j] - a[i] == j - i)
    assert idx_two_keys(a) == idx_brute(a, lambda i, j: j - i == a[i] + a[j])
    assert idx_far_equal(a, d) == idx_brute(a, lambda i, j: a[i] == a[j] and j - i >= d)
assert idx_same_diff([3, 5, 1, 4, 6, 6]) == 1                 # only (3, 5): 6-4 = 5-3
assert idx_two_keys([2, 3, 3, 1, 3, 1]) == 3                  # ABC166 E, first sample
assert idx_far_equal([1, 1, 1, 1], 2) == 3                    # (0,2), (0,3), (1,3)
```

```{python}
iv_a = [2, 3, 3, 1, 3, 1]                                     # 0-based positions here
iv_left = [i + v for i, v in enumerate(iv_a)]
iv_right = [j - v for j, v in enumerate(iv_a)]
iv_match = [sum(1 for i in range(j) if iv_left[i] == iv_right[j]) for j in range(len(iv_a))]
assert iv_match == [0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 2] and sum(iv_match) == 3

                   ["a[j]", *map(str, iv_a)],
```

The first sample of @sec-cnt-pidx-message with 0-based positions. Every position carries two keys; a pair $(i, j)$ qualifies when the *left* key of $i$ equals the *right* key of $j$. At $j = 3$ the right key $2$ meets the left key of $i = 0$; at $j = 5$ the right key $4$ meets the left keys of $i = 1$ and $i = 3$. ## A6. Counting subarrays with a property {#sec-cnt-a4}

**From pairs back to windows.** A window is a pair of cut points, so everything in A4 and A5 applies to windows once the window's property is written as a relation between its two cut points. This lesson collects the relations that come up, and says which tool each one permits.

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Now the window has a *condition* to satisfy, so there is no linearity to exploit and the answer is a genuine **count**. Three framings, in order of generality. **Prefix equality**: "sum equals $K$" is "$P[r+1] - P[l] = K$", i.e. for each $r$ count earlier prefixes equal to $P[r+1] - K$ — one hash map, $O(n)$, and the *only* version that works with negative entries (@sec-pref-hash). **At-most differences**: for non-negative entries, "everything ending at $r$ that is still legal" is a window width $r - \text{left} + 1$, so a shrinking loop counts $\text{atMost}(K)$; then $\text{exactly}(K) = \text{atMost}(K) - \text{atMost}(K-1)$ (@sec-sw-a4). **Runs**: a property that no legal window can cross a bad cell splits the array into runs, and a run of length $L$ holds $\binom{L+1}{2}$ windows. When the *bad* windows are the easy ones to describe, count those and subtract — the subject of @sec-cnt-comp.
:::

Work through the prefix version once by hand and you will never misplace the seed again. For `[1,0,1,0,1]` with goal $2$ the prefix sums are $[0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]$: six values, positions $0..5$ in cut-point space. A window is a pair of cut points $(l, r+1)$, and it is good when the later value exceeds the earlier by exactly $2$. The pairs are $(0,3), (0,4), (1,5), (2,5)$ — four of them, the sample, corresponding to the windows `a[0..2]`, `a[0..3]`, `a[1..4]`, `a[2..4]` — and notice they are *not* pairs of equal values, they are pairs with a fixed difference. That is the whole algorithm: sweep, and for the current prefix $p$ add the count of previously seen prefixes equal to $p - K$. The seed `cnt[0] = 1` is the empty prefix at cut point $0$: without it the windows that start at index $0$ are invisible, and @sec-cnt-p3-binsum's storyboard shows the loss ($2$ instead of $4$).

```{python}
def count_prefix(a, K):
    cnt = {0: 1}                     # the empty prefix: cut point 0
    s = ans = 0
    for v in a:
        s += v
        ans += cnt.get(s - K, 0)     # earlier prefixes exactly K below the current one
        cnt[s] = cnt.get(s, 0) + 1
    return ans


def count_atmost(a, K):
    if K < 0:
        return 0
    left = s = ans = 0
    for right, v in enumerate(a):
        s += v
        while s > K:
            s -= a[left]
            left += 1
        ans += right - left + 1      # every start in left..right is legal
    return ans


assert count_prefix([1, 0, 1, 0, 1], 2) == 4
assert count_atmost([1, 0, 1, 0, 1], 2) - count_atmost([1, 0, 1, 0, 1], 1) == 4
assert count_prefix([1, 1, 1], 2) == 2                      # LC 560's first sample
assert count_prefix([1, -1, 1, -1, 1], 0) == 6              # negatives: still fine
assert count_atmost([1, -1, 1, -1, 1], 0) == 10            # ... and this is the trap
neg = [1, -1, 1, -1, 1]
honest_atmost = sum(1 for i in range(5) for j in range(i, 5) if sum(neg[i:j + 1]) <= 0)
brute = sum(1 for i in range(5) for j in range(i, 5) if sum(neg[i:j + 1]) == 0)
assert honest_atmost == 9 and brute == count_prefix(neg, 0) == 6
# the remainder form of the same idea (LC 974): equality of prefix *residues*
def count_divisible(a, k):
    cnt = {0: 1}
    s = ans = 0
    for v in a:
        s = (s + v) % k
        ans += cnt.get(s, 0)
        cnt[s] = cnt.get(s, 0) + 1
    return ans


assert count_divisible([4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1], 5) == 7
assert count_divisible([5, 0, 0, 0], 3) == 6      # the three zeros give 6 zero-sum windows
# complementary counting: the universe is all windows, and the complement is a partition
n = 5
assert math.comb(n + 1, 2) == 15                  # 15 windows in [1,-1,1,-1,1]
bad = sum(1 for i in range(n) for j in range(i, n) if sum(neg[i:j + 1]) != 0)
assert bad == 15 - count_prefix(neg, 0) == 9
for trial in range(80):
    a = [random.randint(0, 2) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 9))]
    K = random.randint(0, 6)
    b = sum(1 for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i, len(a)) if sum(a[i:j + 1]) == K)
    assert count_prefix(a, K) == b == count_atmost(a, K) - count_atmost(a, K - 1)
```

```{python}
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["index i",              "0", "1", "2", "3", "4"],
                   ["a[i]",                 "1", "0", "1", "0", "1"],
                   ["prefix s",             "1", "1", "2", "2", "3"],
                   ["look for s-K (K=2)",   "-1","-1","0", "0", "1"],
                   ["seen count (charge)",  "0", "0", "1", "1", "2"],
                   ["running answer",       "0", "0", "1", "2", "4"]],
           colors={(3, 3): "cyan", (3, 4): "cyan", (4, 5): "amber", (5, 5): "green"},
           cell_w=1.1)
V.show(draw)
```

Row 4 is the lookup the sweep performs at each step and row 5 is what the map answers: by index $4$ two earlier prefixes equal $s - 2 = 1$ (at cut points $1$ and $2$), so the last element collects the amber $2$ and the running answer in row 6 lands on the green $4$. The two cyan cells are the lookups that found the *seeded* prefix $0$ — they are the windows that start at index $0$, and they exist only because `cnt[0] = 1` was seeded; delete the seed and row 6 finishes at $2$.

:::

The middle assertion in the last loop is the chapter's most useful identity and the trap assertion three lines above it is its most useful *limitation*: $\text{exactly}(K) = \text{atMost}(K) - \text{atMost}(K-1)$ is correct for non-negative arrays and silently wrong the moment a negative appears. The shrink loop rests on the claim "if `a[left..right]` is legal, every shorter suffix of it is too", which is only true when extending a window leftwards can never *lower* the sum. On `[1,-1,1,-1,1]` with $K = 0$ the claim fails: when `right = 4` the loop holds `left = 1` and books four windows ending at $4$, two of which (`a[2..4]` and `a[4..4]`) have sum $1$. The rung answers $10$ where the honest "at most $0$" count is $9$ and the "exactly $0$" count is $6$ — wrong twice, and wrong in both directions. The prefix-hash form has no such assumption: it is $O(n)$ on any integers, which is why LC 560 (with negatives) is a prefix-map problem and LC 930 (binary, so non-negative) can be solved either way, and why @sec-cnt-p3-binsum presents both and compares them.

Modulo is a third framing worth naming explicitly because students lose points on it: "sum divisible by $k$" is prefix *residue* equality, and in C++/Java `(-2) % 5` is $-2$, so the residue must be normalised with `((s % k) + k) % k`. The Python cell above relies on Python's always-non-negative `%`. The book's write-ups of LC 560 and LC 974 live in the prefix-sums chapter (@sec-pref-p2-a and @sec-pref-p2-b); this chapter's job is to tell you *which* of the three framings your condition belongs to, and the decision table is at the end of @sec-cnt-p3.

## A7. Complementary counting {#sec-cnt-comp}

**From the good objects to the bad ones.** Every framing so far counted the objects you want directly. Sometimes the wanted property is an "and" of several conditions, or an "at least one", while its negation is a single simple condition. Then it is cheaper to count **everything** — a number you know in closed form — and subtract the objects that fail.

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Count the whole universe, count the bad part, subtract. The universes have closed forms: $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs, $\binom{n+1}{2}$ subarrays, $\binom{n}{3}$ triples. "At least one $x$ in the window" is hard to track directly but its negation, "no $x$ at all", means the window sits inside a run of non-$x$ cells, and a run of length $L$ holds $\binom{L+1}{2}$ windows. When the bad part is a union of two events — "shares a boy *or* shares a girl" — counting each event and adding counts the objects in both events twice, so you add their intersection back once: $|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|$. That is **inclusion–exclusion**, and complementary counting is its one-event special case.
:::

Why it is exact: the universe $U$ splits into the good set $G$ and the bad set $B = U \setminus G$, with no overlap and nothing left over, so $|G| = |U| - |B|$. For two bad events, an object in $A \cap B$ is counted once in $|A|$ and once in $|B|$, so it must be subtracted once more; an object in exactly one event is counted once. The identity is a statement about how many times each object is counted, which is the contribution technique of @sec-cnt-a1 applied to *membership* instead of values. Three shapes cover most problems:

- **Pairs with different keys** $= \binom{n}{2} - \sum_v \binom{c_v}{2}$, the complement of A4's equal-key count (LC 2364 is this with the key $a_i - i$).
- **Windows containing at least one marked cell** $= \binom{n+1}{2} - \sum_{\text{runs of unmarked cells}} \binom{L+1}{2}$.
- **Windows containing both an $x$ and a $y$** $= \text{all} - \text{no } x - \text{no } y + \text{neither}$; the last term is the intersection that inclusion–exclusion adds back.

```{python}
def comp_brute(a, ok):
    return sum(1 for l in range(len(a)) for r in range(l, len(a)) if ok(a[l:r + 1]))


def comp_runs(a, bad):
    """Windows that avoid every cell with bad(cell): sum of C(L+1, 2) over runs."""
    total = run = 0
    for v in a:
        run = 0 if bad(v) else run + 1
        total += run                          # windows avoiding bad cells that end here
    return total


def comp_at_least_one(a, x):
    n = len(a)
    return n * (n + 1) // 2 - comp_runs(a, lambda v: v == x)


def comp_both(a, x, y):                       # inclusion-exclusion over two bad events
    n = len(a)
    no_x = comp_runs(a, lambda v: v == x)
    no_y = comp_runs(a, lambda v: v == y)
    neither = comp_runs(a, lambda v: v in (x, y))
    return n * (n + 1) // 2 - no_x - no_y + neither


assert comp_at_least_one([1, 0, 2, 2, 0, 3], 0) == 21 - 5 == 16
for _ in range(300):
    a = [random.randint(0, 3) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))]
    assert comp_at_least_one(a, 0) == comp_brute(a, lambda w: 0 in w)
    assert comp_both(a, 1, 2) == comp_brute(a, lambda w: 1 in w and 2 in w)
    n = len(a)
    diff_pairs = sum(1 for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n) if a[i] != a[j])
    assert diff_pairs == math.comb(n, 2) - sum(math.comb(c, 2) for c in Counter(a).values())
```

::: {#fig-cnt-comp}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
cp_a = [1, 0, 2, 2, 0, 3]
assert comp_at_least_one(cp_a, 0) == 16 and comp_runs(cp_a, lambda v: v == 0) == 5


def draw(ax, p):
    V.array(ax, p, cp_a, colors={1: "amber", 4: "amber"},
            regions=[(0, 1, "muted", "L=1: 1"), (2, 4, "cyan", "L=2: 3"),
                     (5, 6, "muted", "L=1: 1")],
            label="a", note="all 21 windows - 5 without a 0 = 16")
V.show(draw)
```

Windows of `[1, 0, 2, 2, 0, 3]` that contain at least one `0` (amber). Instead of tracking zeros inside every window, count the windows that avoid them: they live inside the three runs between the zeros, worth $\binom{2}{2} + \binom{3}{2} + \binom{2}{2} = 1 + 3 + 1 = 5$. All $\binom{7}{2} = 21$ windows minus those $5$ leaves $16$.

:::

The trap is overlap. If the bad events can happen together and you subtract both, the objects in both are subtracted twice; for "contains both $1$ and $2$" the windows containing neither must be added back. When the events are disjoint — "this triple repeats value $v$" for different $v$ in @sec-cnt-pcomp-unequal, or "shares a boy" and "shares a girl" between distinct couples in @sec-cnt-pcomp-ball — the intersection is empty, and the proof that it is empty is part of the solution.

## A8. Triples and small values {#sec-cnt-a5}

**From pairs to triples.** Every structure so far had two free choices: two ends of a window, two members of a pair. A triple $i < j < k$ has three, and the naive loop is $O(n^3)$. The pivot from @sec-tp (fix one element, solve the rest) comes back, but the element to fix is chosen by the *conditions*, and the leftover is a counting question rather than a search.

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Three indices $i < j < k$, three conditions, and the naive answer is $O(n^3)$. The escape is to notice that the conditions are not symmetric: usually **one index appears in two of them**. Pivot on that middle index. If there is no condition between the two outer indices, the left choice and the right choice are independent, and the number of triples with middle $j$ is simply (choices on the left) $\times$ (choices on the right). If there *is* a third condition linking the outer indices, the product overcounts; fix $j$ and $k$, and the condition on $i$ becomes an *interval of values*, which a histogram of the values left of $j$ answers in $O(1)$ with a cumulative table. Either way $O(n^3)$ becomes $O(n^2)$ or better, because you stopped iterating over the object that was expensive to enumerate.
:::

The product case first, on the sample of @sec-cnt-p4-teams: `rating = [2, 5, 3, 4, 1]`, and a team is $i < j < k$ with ratings increasing or decreasing. Both conditions of an increasing team involve $j$ ($r_i < r_j$ and $r_j < r_k$), and nothing relates $r_i$ to $r_k$ directly, so with $j$ fixed every smaller rating on the left pairs with every larger rating on the right. @fig-cnt-anim-middle steps the middle across the array.

::: {#fig-cnt-anim-middle}

```{python}
#| echo: false
mid_r = [2, 5, 3, 4, 1]
mid_states, mid_total = [], 0
mid_states.append(({}, [], "rating = [2, 5, 3, 4, 1]; a team is increasing or decreasing; total = 0"))
for jj in range(1, len(mid_r) - 1):
    lt = [i for i in range(jj) if mid_r[i] < mid_r[jj]]
    gt = [i for i in range(jj) if mid_r[i] > mid_r[jj]]
    rg = [k for k in range(jj + 1, len(mid_r)) if mid_r[k] > mid_r[jj]]
    rl = [k for k in range(jj + 1, len(mid_r)) if mid_r[k] < mid_r[jj]]
    add = len(lt) * len(rg) + len(gt) * len(rl)
    mid_total += add
    colors = {jj: "amber"}
    colors.update({i: "cyan" for i in lt})
    colors.update({k: "green" for k in rg})
    colors.update({i: "pink" for i in gt})
    colors.update({k: "violet" for k in rl})
    mid_states.append((colors, [(jj, "j", "amber")],
                       f"j={jj} (rating {mid_r[jj]}): smaller-left {len(lt)} x larger-right {len(rg)}"
                       f" + larger-left {len(gt)} x smaller-right {len(rl)} = {add}; total = {mid_total}"))
brute_teams = sum(1 for i in range(5) for j in range(i + 1, 5) for k in range(j + 1, 5)
                  if mid_r[i] < mid_r[j] < mid_r[k] or mid_r[i] > mid_r[j] > mid_r[k])
assert mid_total == brute_teams == 3
mid_states.append(({}, [], "the ends cannot be a middle; sum over middles = 0 + 2 + 1 = 3 teams"))


def mid_frame(ax, p, t):
    colors, ptrs, _ = mid_states[t]
    V.array(ax, p, mid_r, colors=dict(colors), pointers=ptrs, label="rating", cell_w=1.2)


V.animate(mid_frame, len(mid_states), captions=[s[2] for s in mid_states], interval=1400)
```

The middle $j$ (amber) walks from index $1$ to index $3$. Cyan cells are smaller ratings on its left and green cells larger ratings on its right — each cyan–green combination is one increasing team; pink (larger, left) and violet (smaller, right) combine into decreasing teams. The counts multiply because nothing links the left choice to the right choice.

:::

@sec-cnt-p4-triplets is the full ladder for the coupled case; here is the shape of the argument with the numbers from its sample. For `arr = [3,0,1,1,9,7]`, $a = 7$, $b = 2$, $c = 3$ there are $4$ good triplets, and they are $(0,1,2), (0,1,3), (0,2,3), (1,2,3)$ — all living in the first four slots. Pivoting on $j$: the charges by middle index are $j = 1 \to 2$ and $j = 2 \to 2$, everything else $0$. For $j = 1$ ($arr[j] = 0$) the two admissible $k$ are $2$ and $3$ (both hold $1$, so $|arr[j] - arr[k]| = 1 \le 2 = b$), and the only $i < j$ is $0$: $|arr[i] - arr[j]| = |3 - 0| = 3 \le 7 = a$ and $|arr[i] - arr[k]| = |3 - 1| = 2 \le 3 = c$ both hold, so each of the two $k$'s contributes $1$ and the row totals $2$. Written as an algorithm with the middle fixed, the inner step is:

$$\#\{i < j : |a_i - a_j| \le a\} \text{ restricted by } |a_i - a_k| \le c
\;=\; \sum_{v \,:\, \max(a_j - a,\; a_k - c,\; 0) \le v \le \min(a_j + a,\; a_k + c,\; V)} \mathrm{left}[v].$$

That is a *range sum over an array indexed by value*, which is one subtraction on a cumulative table.

```{python}
def a5_tri_scan(arr, A, B, C):
    return sum(1 for i in range(len(arr)) for j in range(i + 1, len(arr))
               for k in range(j + 1, len(arr))
               if abs(arr[i] - arr[j]) <= A and abs(arr[j] - arr[k]) <= B
               and abs(arr[i] - arr[k]) <= C)


def a5_tri_middle(arr, A, B, C, VMAX):
    n, ans = len(arr), 0
    left = [0] * (VMAX + 1)                 # histogram of values strictly left of j
    left[arr[0]] += 1
    for j in range(1, n - 1):
        cum = [0] * (VMAX + 2)              # cum[x] = #left values < x
        for v in range(VMAX + 1):
            cum[v + 1] = cum[v] + left[v]
        for k in range(j + 1, n):
            if abs(arr[j] - arr[k]) > B:
                continue
            lo = max(0, arr[j] - A, arr[k] - C)      # clamp: no negative addressing
            hi = min(VMAX, arr[j] + A, arr[k] + C)
            if lo <= hi:
                ans += cum[hi + 1] - cum[lo]
        left[arr[j]] += 1
    return ans


assert a5_tri_scan([3, 0, 1, 1, 9, 7], 7, 2, 3) == 4
assert a5_tri_middle([3, 0, 1, 1, 9, 7], 7, 2, 3, 1000) == 4
assert a5_tri_scan([0, 0, 0], 0, 0, 0) == 1                 # only (0,1,2)
assert a5_tri_middle([0, 0, 0], 0, 0, 0, 1000) == 1
assert a5_tri_scan([1, 1, 1, 1], 0, 0, 0) == 4              # every triple of four slots
assert math.comb(4, 3) == 4
# when does fixing the middle beat three loops? count the primitive steps.
# rung 2 rebuilds a cumulative table of VMAX+2 cells per middle index and then walks k,
# so its work is (n-2)(VMAX+2) + (number of (j,k) pairs) against binom(n,3) for rung 1.
def a5_steps_middle(n, VMAX):
    return (n - 2) * (VMAX + 2) + sum(n - 1 - j for j in range(1, n - 1))


assert a5_steps_middle(6, 1000) == 4018 > math.comb(6, 3) == 20       # rung 1 wins early
assert a5_steps_middle(78, 1000) == 79078 > math.comb(78, 3) == 76076  # still behind
assert a5_steps_middle(80, 1000) == 81237 < math.comb(80, 3) == 82160  # crossover
assert a5_steps_middle(100, 1000) == 103047 < math.comb(100, 3) == 161700
assert a5_steps_middle(1000, 1000) == 1498497 < math.comb(1000, 3) == 166167000
first_win = {V: min(n for n in range(3, 400) if a5_steps_middle(n, V) < math.comb(n, 3))
             for V in (26, 500, 1000)}
assert first_win == {26: 16, 500: 57, 1000: 80}
for trial in range(40):
    arr = [random.randint(0, 12) for _ in range(random.randint(3, 9))]
    A, B, C = (random.randint(0, 6) for _ in range(3))
    assert a5_tri_scan(arr, A, B, C) == a5_tri_middle(arr, A, B, C, 1000)
```

::: {#fig-cnt-a5}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["middle j",              "1",  "2",  "3", "4"],
                   ["arr[j]",                "0",  "1",  "1", "9"],
                   ["k with |arr[j]-arr[k]|<=2", "{2,3}", "{3}", "-", "{5}"],
                   ["i counted for each k",  "{0}", "{0,1}", "-", "{}"],
                   ["charge",                "2",  "2",  "0", "0"]],
           colors={(2, 1): "cyan", (2, 2): "cyan", (4, 1): "amber", (4, 2): "amber",
                   (3, 4): "muted", (2, 4): "muted"},
           cell_w=1.5)
V.show(draw)
```

With $j$ fixed the two remaining conditions split cleanly: row 3 lists the $k$'s that pass the *middle-to-right* test $|arr[j] - arr[k]| \le b$, and row 4 answers the *left* test with one lookup over the value histogram — for $j = 2$ both $i = 0$ and $i = 1$ are eligible, and the table says so in $O(1)$ instead of a loop. The charges in row 5 add to the sample's $4$. The two muted cells are the $j = 4$ column: $|9 - 7| = 2 \le b$ does admit $k = 5$, but then no $i$ survives both $|arr[i] - 9| \le 7$ and $|arr[i] - 7| \le 3$ (the only candidate, $i = 0$, fails the second with $|3 - 7| = 4$), so the interval is empty and the charge is $0$. At $j = 3$ even the $k$ test fails for both remaining values.

:::

Two general lessons sit inside those lines. **"Index condition" versus "value condition."** $i < j < k$ is a condition on *positions*; $|a_i - a_j| \le 7$ is a condition on *values*. Position conditions are handled by the order in which you loop (fix $j$ and everything to its left is automatically eligible), and value conditions are handled by a table over values — the same division of labour as @sec-cnt-idxval, where the order of insertion enforced $j - i \ge d$. A problem that mixes them wants exactly this split — and @sec-cnt-p4-xortri shows the degenerate case where a value condition ($a == b$) *eliminates* the middle index entirely, so the pivot moves to the ends and the free middle contributes a multiplicative $k - i$.

**Small values are a gift: let the value be the address.** The cumulative table above is $O(V)$ to rebuild and $O(1)$ to query, and it is affordable only because $V = 1000$. Whenever you see "$1 \le arr[i] \le 500$" or "lowercase letters only", the statement is offering you an array of $500$ or $26$ cells indexed by *value* — @sec-lts-a5, and the reason @sec-cnt-p5-lucky can answer "which value occurs exactly as many times as itself?" with a table sweep, and @sec-cnt-p5-beauty can decide a maximum and minimum frequency by cursors over frequency buckets instead of a scan. Two arithmetic facts to keep handy. First, a table over values costs $O(V)$ to rebuild, so the fixed-middle rung is $O(nV + n^2)$ — which is why the crossover depends on $V$ and not only on $n$: with $V = 1000$ the rung starts winning at $n = 80$, with $V = 500$ at $n = 57$, and with an alphabet-sized $V = 26$ at $n = 16$. Second, a *count* table can be indexed by the count itself: if $\mathrm{cnt}[v] == v$ then the value $v$ occupies $v$ slots and therefore consumes $v^2$ of the array's $n$ cells, so $\sum_{v\ \text{lucky}} v^2 \le n$ — at $n = 500$ at most $10$ values can be lucky, since $1^2 + \cdots + 10^2 = 385 \le 500 < 506 = 1^2 + \cdots + 11^2$.

## Part B — Patterns

## Pattern 1: The contribution swap — charge the elements, not the windows {#sec-cnt-p1}

**Where we are.** The eight patterns of Part B climb one idea at a time. Pattern 1 sums over all **windows** by charging each element its cover count. Pattern 2 sums over all **pairs** the same way. Pattern 3 stops summing and starts *counting* pairs, and Pattern 4 lets the indices into the pair condition. Pattern 5 returns to windows, now counted by a property. Pattern 6 counts the complement when the property is easier to violate than to satisfy. Pattern 7 adds a third index and fixes the middle one. Pattern 8 notices that small values turn every table in the chapter into a plain array. Pattern 1 is where the reframing starts: A1's dot product is the entire pattern, and its two problems differ in one question — *is the thing you are adding linear in the elements?* The first is the pure case, a sum of sums filtered only by window length, so the cover count changes and nothing else does. The second breaks linearity on purpose: its statistic is $\max - \min$, so the credit has to be re-derived as "the windows in which this slot wins", which is A2's spans.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Never enumerate the object you were asked to iterate over — enumerate the object that is *fewer*:

- Slot $i$ of an $n$-cell array is covered by $(i+1)(n-i)$ subarrays, so $\sum_{\text{windows}} \text{sum} = \sum_i a_i (i+1)(n-i)$ in one pass (@eq-cnt-swap).
- A *filter* on the window (odd length, a length range) changes only how many of those covering windows count — for odd length it is $\lceil (i+1)(n-i)/2 \rceil$.
- A *non-linear statistic* ($\max$, $\max - \min$) changes the credit into "windows in which $i$ is the winner", a product of two monotonic-stack spans with opposite tie-breaking (@sec-cnt-a2).
:::

::: {#fig-cnt-anim-p1}

```{python}
#| echo: false
p1_arr = Traces.OS_ARR                       # [1, 4, 2, 5, 3]
p1_cover = [((i + 1) * (len(p1_arr) - i) + 1) // 2 for i in range(len(p1_arr))]
p1_credit = [v * c for v, c in zip(p1_arr, p1_cover)]
assert p1_cover == [3, 4, 5, 4, 3] and sum(p1_credit) == 58
p1_states = [
    ([str(v) for v in p1_arr], {}, "rung 1: add up the 9 odd-length windows, one window per loop"),
    ([str(c) for c in p1_cover], {i: "cyan" for i in range(5)},
     "re-index: how many odd-length windows cover each slot"),
    ([str(c) for c in p1_credit], {i: "green" for i in range(5)},
     "credit = value x cover; 3+16+10+20+9 = 58, one pass"),
]


def p1_frame(ax, p, t):
    cells, colours, _ = p1_states[t]
    V.array(ax, p, cells, colors=dict(colours), label=["arr", "odd cover", "credit"][t])


V.animate(p1_frame, 3, captions=[s[2] for s in p1_states], interval=1200)
```

The film is a change of *what the array means*. Frame 1 is the input, whose definition asks for a loop over its $9$ odd-length windows; frame 2 replaces each value by its odd-window cover count $[3, 4, 5, 4, 3]$; frame 3 multiplies the two. $58$ is the answer @sec-cnt-p1-oddsum works out from its statement's example, reached without naming a single window.

:::

**Reading the animation.** Cover counts are a *shape*, not data: $[3, 4, 5, 4, 3]$ depends only on $n = 5$, so you can compute them once, cache them, or — the trick every final form in this pattern uses — generate them inside the loop as `(i + 1) * (n - i)`. The odd-length filter is the one wrinkle worth memorising: of the windows covering a slot, the odd-length ones are half, rounded up when $(i+1)(n-i)$ is odd, so the count is $\lceil (i+1)(n-i)/2 \rceil$. @sec-cnt-p1-oddsum walks that ladder ($O(n^3)$ rescan $\to$ prefix sums $\to$ cover counts); @sec-cnt-p1-ranges then takes the swap to the case where it is *not* directly legal and rebuilds the credit from spans.

{{< include ../problems/lc-1588-sum-of-all-odd-length-subarrays/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a linear statistic to an extremal one.** 1588 adds element values, so each element's contribution is its value times a cover count that depends only on position. 2104 asks for $\max - \min$ per window, and a maximum is not a sum — the cover count must be re-derived as "windows in which this slot is the appointed winner", which is a product of two distances a monotonic stack measures.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-2104-sum-of-subarray-ranges/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 2: Sums over all pairs — split the pair into per-element charges {#sec-cnt-psum}

**From windows to pairs.** Pattern 1 charged each element for the windows that cover it. A pair has two members instead of a range of cells, so the charge of an element depends on its partner, and the swap needs one more step: arrange the partners so their effect is a count. For bitwise quantities that step is "one bit column at a time"; for distances it is "sort, so every difference has a known sign" (@sec-cnt-pairsum). The first problem uses bits, where each column is a two-colour split and the count is $c(n-c)$. The second needs sorting, because a coordinate is a number, not a bit, and it adds grouping by colour and splitting by axis on top.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
$\sum_{i<j} f(a_i, a_j)$ without the double loop:

- **Separable $f$.** $\sum_{i<j}(a_i + a_j) = (n-1)\sum a$; $\sum_{i<j} a_i a_j = \tfrac12\bigl((\sum a)^2 - \sum a^2\bigr)$.
- **Distance $|a_i - a_j|$.** Sort; the element of rank $k$ has weight $2k - n + 1$ (@eq-cnt-rank), or sweep with `total += k * x - prefix`.
- **Bitwise $f$.** Per bit $b$ with $c_b$ ones: XOR pays $2^b c_b(n - c_b)$, AND pays $2^b \binom{c_b}{2}$, OR pays $2^b\bigl(\binom{n}{2} - \binom{n - c_b}{2}\bigr)$.
- **Sum of independent parts** (Manhattan distance, Hamming distance): split, solve each part, add.
:::

{{< include ../problems/lc-0477-total-hamming-distance/problem.qmd >}}

[**From bits to coordinates.** 477's columns are bits, so a pair either differs in a column or not, and $c(n-c)$ is the whole count. 1648A's columns are coordinates, so a pair differs by an *amount*; sorting turns that amount into "later minus earlier", and the count becomes a rank weight.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-1648a-weird-sum/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 3: Counting pairs — fix one end, or close a histogram {#sec-cnt-p2}

**From summing to counting.** Pattern 2 added up a quantity over every pair. Now each pair contributes $1$ or $0$ — it satisfies a relation or not — and the job is to count the $1$s. A4's two shapes are both "count pairs without the double loop", and the choice between them is a property of the relation, not a style preference. The first problem is the relation $a_i = a_j$ with $i < j$ — an equivalence, so both shapes work and the write-up shows the same total arriving by both. The second adds arithmetic: the condition is $(t_i + t_j) \bmod 60 = 0$, which pairs each residue class with its *complementary* class, and two classes ($r = 0$ and $r = 30$) pair with themselves.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
A pair is one loop shorter than a window, and the loop you delete is the inner one:

- **Fix the right end.** Sweep $j$ left-to-right keeping `seen[value]`; on arrival `ans += seen[complement]`, then insert $a_j$ (@sec-cnt-a3). This respects $i < j$ and works for asymmetric relations.
- **Or close a histogram.** If compatibility is an equivalence relation, count $c$ per class once and add $\binom{c}{2}$ — no order, no sweep.
- **Modular conditions**: key the map by $t \bmod k$ and look up $(-t) \bmod k$; residues $0$ and $k/2$ (when $k$ is even) self-pair, so their class is $\binom{c}{2}$, not $c^2$.
- **Range conditions** ($l \le a_i + a_j \le r$): sort and count with two pointers, as below.
:::

::: {#fig-cnt-anim-p2}

```{python}
#| echo: false
p2_arr = Traces.GP_NUMS                     # [1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 3]
p2_seen, p2_charges = Counter(), []
for v in p2_arr:
    p2_charges.append(p2_seen[v])
    p2_seen[v] += 1
assert p2_charges == [0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 1] and sum(p2_charges) == 4
assert sum(math.comb(c, 2) for c in p2_seen.values()) == 4
p2_states = [
    ({3: "amber", 0: "cyan"}, "arrive at j=3 (value 1): one earlier 1, charge 1; running total 1"),
    ({4: "amber", 0: "cyan", 3: "cyan"}, "j=4 (value 1): two earlier 1s, charge 2; running total 3"),
    ({5: "amber", 2: "cyan"}, "j=5 (value 3): one earlier 3, charge 1; running total 4"),
    (None, "histogram {1: 3, 2: 1, 3: 2}: C(3,2) + C(1,2) + C(2,2) = 3 + 0 + 1 = 4"),
]


def p2_frame(ax, p, t):
    colours, _ = p2_states[t]
    if colours is not None:
        V.array(ax, p, p2_arr, colors=dict(colours), label="nums")
    else:
        V.bars(ax, p, [p2_seen[1], p2_seen[2], p2_seen[3]], height=3.0,
               colors={0: "cyan", 2: "green"}, index=False)
        for c, lab in enumerate(["v=1", "v=2", "v=3"]):
            V.text(ax, p, c + 0.5, -0.5, lab, size=9, color="muted")


V.animate(p2_frame, 4, captions=[s[1] for s in p2_states], interval=1300)
```

Frames 1–3 are the sweep: each amber cursor is charged by the cyan cells to its left that hold the same value. Frame 4 is the histogram: the three bars $[3, 1, 2]$ close to $\binom{3}{2} + \binom{1}{2} + \binom{2}{2} = 4$. Two bookkeeping schemes, one answer, because "good pair" is symmetric here.

:::

**Reading the animation.** Frames 1–3 are the sweep and frame 4 is the histogram, and the point of putting them in one film is that *neither is a loop over pairs*: both are $O(n)$ with a different constant. The sweep charges a pair the moment its right end appears, which is why it survives asymmetric relations (inversions, or the two-key condition of @sec-cnt-pidx-message) and the histogram does not (@sec-cnt-a3's `[3,1,2,1]` counterexample). @sec-cnt-p2-goodpairs builds the equivalence case from both sides; @sec-cnt-p2-songs then changes the lookup from "the same value" to "the complementary residue".

{{< include ../problems/lc-1512-number-of-good-pairs/problem.qmd >}}

[**From "equal values" to "complementary residues".** Good pairs ask for `seen[v]` — the class you are already in. Song pairs ask for `seen[(60 - r) % 60]`: the same one-loop sweep with a lookup two characters different, and two classes (residues $0$ and $30$) that must be paired *within* themselves rather than across, which is where a careless $c \cdot c'$ double-counts.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-1010-pairs-of-songs-with-total-durations-divisible-by-60/problem.qmd >}}

When the relation is a *range* of sums rather than one exact complement, no single key answers it. The two-pointer chapter counts those pairs after sorting: "$l \le a_i + a_j \le r$" is "sum $\le r$" minus "sum $\le l - 1$", and each one-sided count is one squeeze. That problem is solved in full there; here is its card, as the third shape of pair counting.

{{< include ../problems/cf-1538c-number-of-pairs/card.qmd >}}

## Pattern 4: Index and value conditions — give each index a key {#sec-cnt-pidx}

**From values to indices.** Pattern 3's relations looked only at values. Now the index is part of the condition, and the first move is algebra: rewrite the condition until one side mentions only $i$ and the other only $j$ (@sec-cnt-idxval). When the two sides are the same function you are back to a histogram — the hashing chapter solved exactly that case, and its card is below. The first new problem has two *different* functions on the two sides, so the sweep must read one key and write the other. The second cannot be separated at all, and a bound on the values replaces the separation.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Rewrite the condition, then pick the counting shape:

- **One key on both sides** ($a_i - i = a_j - j$): group by the key, $\sum \binom{c}{2}$.
- **Two keys** ($i + a_i = j - a_j$): sweep $j$; `ans += cnt[rightkey(j)]`, then `cnt[leftkey(j)] += 1`. Keys that can never be matched may be dropped, which often turns the map into an array.
- **No separation, but a bound** ($a_i a_j = i + j < 2n$): enumerate only the candidates the bound allows — multiples, residue classes — and pay a harmonic sum $O(n \log n)$ when the values are distinct.
- **A distance between indices** ($j - i \ge d$): delay the insertion of $a_{j-d}$ until the cursor reaches $j$.
:::

{{< include ../problems/cf-1520d-same-differences/card.qmd >}}

{{< include ../problems/ac-abc166_e-this-message-will-self-destruct-in-5s/problem.qmd >}}

[**From two keys to no keys.** ABC 166 E splits into $i + A_i$ and $j - A_j$, so a map does the matching. Pleasant Pairs ties a *product* of values to a *sum* of indices, which no rearrangement splits; what saves it is that the product must stay below $2n$.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-1541b-pleasant-pairs/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 5: Windows with a property — equality, at-most, or runs {#sec-cnt-p3}

**From pairs of elements to pairs of cut points.** Patterns 3 and 4 counted pairs of elements. A window is a pair of *cut points*, so the same tools count windows once the property is written as a relation between the two cut points — a fixed difference of prefix sums, an equal residue, or "no bad cell in between". The first problem is unusually instructive because *two* framings apply to the same input and must be made to agree. The second drops the sum entirely: the property is "every character is a `1`", which is a statement about runs, and the count comes from a run-length decomposition plus $\binom{L+1}{2}$ — the same arithmetic as the odd-length window count in @sec-cnt-a1, arriving from a different direction.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Read the condition first, then choose the object to hash:

- **Fixed difference among prefixes.** "sum $= K$" is $P[\text{right}] - P[\text{left}] = K$: sweep, `ans += cnt[p - K]`, `cnt[p] += 1`, seeded `cnt[0] = 1` (@sec-pref-hash). Works with negatives.
- **Residue equality.** "divisible by $k$" is the same sweep with `p % k` and `ans += cnt[p]`; normalise the residue in C++/Java.
- **At-most difference.** For non-negative entries only: $\text{exactly}(K) = \text{atMost}(K) - \text{atMost}(K-1)$, each from one shrinking loop (@sec-sw-a4).
- **Runs.** "all `1`s": decompose into maximal runs and count inside each, $\sum_{\text{runs}} \binom{L+1}{2}$, or stream it as `cur = cur + 1 if good else 0; ans += cur`.
:::

The prefix sweep is drawn step by step in @fig-cnt-a4, and the three framings each have a home write-up already. The two prefix-map problems are solved in the prefix-sums chapter and the at-most difference with a distinct-count window in the sliding-window chapter; their cards stand here as the reference shapes, and the two new problems below are the ones where the framings meet.

{{< include ../problems/lc-0560-subarray-sum-equals-k/card.qmd >}}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0974-subarray-sums-divisible-by-k/card.qmd >}}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0992-subarrays-with-k-different-integers/card.qmd >}}

The one-line diagnostic for which framing you are allowed to use is *does the array contain negatives?* Prefix equality does not care; `atMost` does, because its shrink loop is a monotonicity argument (@sec-cnt-a4's trap). @sec-cnt-p3-binsum therefore ships both and cross-checks them, and its storyboard is where the missing seed shows up as an answer of $2$ instead of $4$. @sec-cnt-p3-ones then removes the sum altogether — the object counted is a run, and a run of length $L$ is worth $\binom{L+1}{2}$ windows whether you materialise the runs or stream `cur`.

{{< include ../problems/lc-0930-binary-subarrays-with-sum/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a sum condition to a shape condition.** 930 asks what a window *adds up to*, so the key is a prefix value. 1513 asks what a window *is made of* — all `1`s — and that is local: a window cannot cross a `0`, so the universe splits into runs and the count is one $\binom{L+1}{2}$ per run. Same re-indexing reflex, different object.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-1513-number-of-substrings-with-only-1s/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 6: Complementary counting — count the bad, subtract {#sec-cnt-pcomp}

**From counting what you want to counting what you do not.** Pattern 5's runs counted windows that *avoid* a bad cell — and "avoid" is half of a complement. Here the complement is the whole strategy (@sec-cnt-comp): the universe has a closed form, the bad objects are described by one simple condition, and the answer is the difference. The first problem's bad events (one value repeated, for different values) are disjoint, so one subtraction per value is exact. The second has two bad events that could overlap, and inclusion–exclusion has to check the overlap.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- Universe: $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs, $\binom{n+1}{2}$ windows, $\binom{n}{3}$ triples.
- **One bad event, or disjoint ones**: answer $= |U| - \sum |B_v|$.
- **Two overlapping bad events**: answer $= |U| - |A| - |B| + |A \cap B|$; prove what $A \cap B$ is (often empty).
- **"At least one"** is the complement of "none", and "none" in a window means "inside a run of good cells": $\binom{n+1}{2} - \sum_{\text{runs}} \binom{L+1}{2}$.
:::

{{< include ../problems/lc-2475-number-of-unequal-triplets-in-array/problem.qmd >}}

[**From disjoint bad events to overlapping ones.** In 2475 a triplet repeats at most one value, so the bad sets for different values never meet and plain subtraction is exact. In Ball in Berland a pair of couples can be bad for two reasons — a shared boy or a shared girl — and the solution must say what happens when both reasons hold.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-1475c-ball-in-berland/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 7: Fix the middle — triples as left counts times right counts {#sec-cnt-p4}

**From pairs to triples.** Patterns 3–5 counted objects with two free choices, and Pattern 6 met triples only through groups of values. A triple has three, and A8's pivot is the pattern: fix the index that appears in two of the three conditions. The three problems are its three cases. In the first, nothing links the outer indices, so the left and right counts simply multiply (@fig-cnt-anim-middle). In the second, a third condition links them, so the product overcounts and an interval query over values takes its place. In the third, the condition says nothing about the middle at all, so the middle is free and contributes a multiplicative factor instead of a loop.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Three indices, three conditions: **find the index that appears in two of them and fix it**.

- **No condition between the ends**: answer $= \sum_j \text{left}_j \cdot \text{right}_j$ (@sec-cnt-p4-teams).
- **A condition between the ends**: with $j$ and $k$ pinned, the admissible $a_i$ are an *interval of values* — one subtraction on a cumulative table over the left histogram (@sec-cnt-a5). Keep the histogram moving with $j$ (`left[arr[j]] += 1` after processing $j$), and clamp the interval to $[0, V]$ before indexing.
- **A condition that ignores the middle**: pivot on the ends, count the pairs of ends that work and multiply by the number of free middles.
:::

::: {#fig-cnt-anim-p4}

```{python}
#| echo: false
p4_arr = list(Traces.GT_ARR)                 # [3, 0, 1, 1, 9, 7]
p4_charge = []
for jj in range(1, len(p4_arr) - 1):
    p4_charge.append(sum(1 for i in range(jj) for k in range(jj + 1, len(p4_arr))
                         if abs(p4_arr[i] - p4_arr[jj]) <= 7 and abs(p4_arr[jj] - p4_arr[k]) <= 2
                         and abs(p4_arr[i] - p4_arr[k]) <= 3))
assert p4_charge == [2, 2, 0, 0] and sum(p4_charge) == 4
p4_states = [
    ({1: "amber"}, [(1, "j", "amber")], "fix j=1 (value 0): k must satisfy |0 - arr[k]| <= 2, so k in {2, 3}"),
    ({1: "amber", 2: "green", 0: "cyan"}, [(1, "j", "amber"), (2, "k", "green")],
     "k=2: arr[i] must lie in [max(0-7, 1-3), min(0+7, 1+3)] = [-2, 4], clamped to [0, 4]; the left pool {3} has 1 hit"),
    ({4: "amber", 5: "green"}, [(4, "j", "amber"), (5, "k", "green")],
     "j=4, k=5 pass |9-7| <= 2, but [max(2, 4), min(16, 10)] = [4, 10] holds none of {3, 0, 1, 1}"),
    (None, None, "charges by middle: j=1 -> 2, j=2 -> 2, j=3 -> 0, j=4 -> 0; total 4"),
]


def p4_frame(ax, p, t):
    colours, ptrs, _ = p4_states[t]
    if colours is not None:
        V.array(ax, p, p4_arr, colors=dict(colours), pointers=ptrs, label="arr")
    else:
        V.bars(ax, p, p4_charge, height=3.0, colors={0: "green", 1: "green"}, index=False)
        for c, lab in enumerate(["j=1", "j=2", "j=3", "j=4"]):
            V.text(ax, p, c + 0.5, -0.5, lab, size=9, color="muted")


V.animate(p4_frame, 4, captions=[s[2] for s in p4_states], interval=1500)
```
