The coupled case on @sec-cnt-p4-triplets' sample ($a = 7$, $b = 2$, $c = 3$). With $j$ and $k$ fixed the third condition becomes an interval of values for $a_i$; frame 3 shows a pair $(j, k)$ that passes its own test and still gets nothing, because the interval misses every value on the left. The last frame is the whole answer by middle index.

:::

**Reading the animation.** Compare it with @fig-cnt-anim-middle: there the left and right counts were independent and multiplied; here frame 3 is exactly the case where multiplying would be wrong, since $(3, 9, 7)$ passes the two chain conditions and fails the closing one. @sec-cnt-p4-teams is the product case, @sec-cnt-p4-triplets walks rescan $\to$ value scan $\to$ cumulative table, and @sec-cnt-p4-xortri is the degenerate pivot, where an XOR identity ($a == b \iff a \oplus b == 0$) deletes the middle entirely and leaves pairs of equal prefix XORs, each worth $k - i$ triplets.

{{< include ../problems/lc-1395-count-number-of-teams/problem.qmd >}}

[**From independent sides to coupled sides.** In Count Number of Teams nothing relates the left soldier to the right one, so the counts multiply. Count Good Triplets adds $|arr[i] - arr[k]| \le c$, a condition between the ends; the product would overcount, and the fix is to pin $k$ too and turn the condition on $i$ into an interval of values.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-1534-count-good-triplets/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a pivot that pays to a pivot that vanishes.** 1534 needs the middle: it is where two of the three conditions meet. 1442's condition lives only at the two ends, so the middle is free — and the cleverness is not the histogram but the identity that turns "$a == b$" into "the XOR of the whole span is $0$", which is the prefix XOR of @sec-pref-other.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-1442-count-triplets-that-can-form-two-arrays-of-equal-xor/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 8: Small values — let the value be the address {#sec-cnt-p5}

**From index tables to value tables.** Every pattern so far stored counts in a map keyed by a value, a residue or a computed key. A8's last paragraph is this pattern: a stated bound on values is an offer of a plain array indexed by value. The first problem takes the offer literally ($1 \le arr[i] \le 500$, so a $501$-cell table replaces a search). The second takes it one level up — the *counts* are small too ($\le 500$), so a table indexed by frequency answers "what is the largest and smallest frequency in this window?" without sorting anything, the counter-of-counters design of @sec-ds used inside a window.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **Bounded values → direct address.** `cnt[v]` in $O(1)$ with no hashing (@sec-lts-a5); sweep the table when the question quantifies over *values* rather than positions.
- **A condition like $\mathrm{cnt}[v] == v$** is checked by walking the finished table, and the answer's shape ("largest such $v$") decides the sweep direction: ascending with `best = v`, or descending and return on the first hit.
- **Counter of counters.** When the question is about a frequency, index a bucket table by frequency (`how[f]`) and keep `maxf`/`minf` cursors; a bucket can only be judged once its value stops changing.
:::

::: {#fig-cnt-p5}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
p5_in = list(Traces.LUCK_ARR)                 # [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]
p5_cnt = [p5_in.count(v) for v in (1, 2, 3)]
assert p5_cnt == [1, 2, 3] and max(v for v, c in zip((1, 2, 3), p5_cnt) if c == v) == 3


def draw(ax, p):
    V.array(ax, p, p5_in, x=0.0, y=4.6, label="arr")
    V.bars(ax, p, p5_cnt, x=0.5, y=0.0, height=3.0, colors={0: "green", 1: "green", 2: "green"},
           index=False)
    for c, lab in enumerate(["v=1", "v=2", "v=3"]):
        V.text(ax, p, c + 1.0, -0.5, lab, size=9, color="muted")
    V.text(ax, p, 4.2, 1.5, "cnt[v] == v for v = 1, 2, 3; largest is 3", ha="left", size=9,
           color="muted")
V.show(draw)
```

The bars are the count table, not the input: the six values fill three buckets, and every bucket passes the test $\mathrm{cnt}[v] = v$, so the largest lucky value is $3$ — LC 1394's sample. The table has $501$ cells, and the bound $\sum_{v \text{ lucky}} v^2 \le n$ of @sec-cnt-a5 says no more than $10$ of them can ever pass when $n = 500$.

:::

**Reading the figure.** Two habits are being trained here. First, *re-read the constraint line for a bound on values*, because it converts a search into an array walk: @sec-cnt-p5-lucky goes `arr.count(v)` per distinct value (an $O(n \cdot d)$ rescan that is still fast at $n = 500$) $\to$ sorted runs $\to$ the direct table. Second, when the quantity is itself a count, index *by* it: @sec-cnt-p5-beauty's windows have frequencies $\le 500$, so `how[f]` plus two cursors turns "max frequency minus min frequency" into $O(1)$ per window instead of a scan of $26$ cells — and the subtlety is entirely in when a cursor is allowed to move.

{{< include ../problems/lc-1394-find-lucky-integer-in-an-array/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a table indexed by value to a table indexed by count.** 1394 asks a question about a value and its own frequency, so one direct-address table answers it. 1781 asks about the *spread of frequencies* inside every substring: the values are only $26$ letters, but the interesting array is now `how[f]` — a counter of counters, with a reset on each new letter's first arrival.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-1781-sum-of-beauty-of-all-substrings/problem.qmd >}}

**Looking back.** One sentence ran through all eight patterns: *count by contribution — decide which object to iterate over, and charge everything else to it.* Pattern 1 iterated over elements and charged them windows; Pattern 2 iterated over elements, bits or ranks and charged them pairs; Patterns 3 and 4 iterated over right ends and charged them their earlier partners, after rewriting the condition into keys; Pattern 5 iterated over cut points; Pattern 6 iterated over the bad objects because there were fewer kinds of them; Pattern 7 iterated over middles and charged them products or interval counts; Pattern 8 iterated over values because there were fewer values than positions. Each time the answer had to be *exact*, and each time the check was the same: a brute force on small inputs and a second framing that must agree.

## Pattern map

Every row is the same decision — *which object do I iterate over?* — taken against a different
shape of statement.

| Signal in the statement | Pattern | Section |
|---|---|---|
| "Sum of `sum(arr[i..j])` over all subarrays" | Contribution swap: charge slot $i$ with $(i+1)(n-i)$ | @sec-cnt-a1, @sec-cnt-p1 |
| "Sum over all **odd-length** subarrays" | Same swap, cover count $\lceil (i+1)(n-i)/2 \rceil$ | @sec-cnt-p1-oddsum |
| "Sum of ranges / of maxima / of minima of all subarrays" | Credit the *winner*: product of two monotonic-stack spans, opposite tie-breaking | @sec-cnt-a2, @sec-cnt-p1-ranges |
| "Sum of $|a_i - a_j|$ / of products / of XORs over all pairs" | Sort and weight by rank $2k - n + 1$; expand the square; count ones per bit, $c(n-c)$ | @sec-cnt-pairsum, @sec-cnt-psum |
| "Sum of distances over same-coloured pairs of cells" | Group by colour, split into coordinates, sort each | @sec-cnt-psum-weird |
| "Count pairs with `nums[i] == nums[j]`, $i < j$" | Fix the right end and charge `seen[v]`, or close the group with $\binom{c}{2}$ | @sec-cnt-a3, @sec-cnt-p2-goodpairs |
| "Count pairs with $(t_i + t_j) \bmod k = 0$" | Residue histogram + complementary bucket; $r=0$ and $r=k/2$ self-pair | @sec-cnt-p2-songs |
| "Count pairs with $l \le a_i + a_j \le r$" | Sort; two one-sided counts with two pointers | @sec-tp |
| "Count pairs with $a_j - a_i = j - i$" | One key on both sides, $a_i - i$; histogram | @sec-cnt-idxval, @sec-hash |
| "Count pairs with $j - i = a_i + a_j$" | Two keys, $i + a_i$ and $j - a_j$; fix the right end | @sec-cnt-pidx-message |
| "Count pairs with $a_i \cdot a_j = i + j$, values distinct and $\le 2n$" | Enumerate the residue class of $j$; harmonic sum | @sec-cnt-pidx-pleasant |
| "Count subarrays with sum $= K$ (values may be negative)" | Prefix equality in a hash map, seeded `cnt[0] = 1` | @sec-cnt-a4, @sec-pref-p2-a |
| "Count subarrays divisible by $k$" | The same sweep keyed on `prefix % k` | @sec-pref-p2-b |
| "Count subarrays with **exactly** $K$ of something (non-negative)" | $\text{atMost}(K) - \text{atMost}(K-1)$, one shrinking window each | @sec-cnt-a4, @sec-cnt-p3-binsum |
| "Count substrings that are all `1`" | Split into runs, $\sum_{\text{runs}} \binom{L+1}{2}$ | @sec-cnt-p3-ones |
| "Count windows containing at least one $x$" / "both $x$ and $y$" | Complement: all windows minus the runs that avoid $x$; inclusion–exclusion for two | @sec-cnt-comp |
| "Count triples with pairwise **distinct** values" | $\binom{n}{3}$ minus the triples that repeat a value | @sec-cnt-pcomp-unequal |
| "Count pairs of objects sharing **no** attribute" | $\binom{k}{2}$ minus same-attribute pairs, plus the overlap | @sec-cnt-pcomp-ball |
| "Count increasing (or decreasing) triples $i < j < k$" | Fix the middle: smaller-left $\times$ larger-right | @sec-cnt-a5, @sec-cnt-p4-teams |
| "Count triples $(i, j, k)$ with three pairwise value conditions" | Fix the middle; the rest is one interval query on a value histogram | @sec-cnt-a5, @sec-cnt-p4-triplets |
| "Count triplets with $a == b$ where $a, b$ are XORs of the two halves" | The middle cancels: count zero-XOR windows, weight each by $k - i$ | @sec-cnt-p4-xortri |
| "$1 \le arr[i] \le 500$ and a condition like $\mathrm{cnt}[v] = v$" | Direct addressing: let the value be the address and sweep the table | @sec-cnt-a5, @sec-cnt-p5-lucky |
| "Sum of a spread of *frequencies* over all windows" | Counter of counters `how[f]` plus two cursors | @sec-cnt-p5-beauty |
| "The answer is a count of $\binom{n+1}{2}$-sized things and $n \ge 10^5$" | Any of the above — the double loop is not the answer | @sec-cnt-why |

## Pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Forgetting the `cnt[0] = 1` seed.** The prefix *before the first element* is a legal left end, and a map that starts empty cannot see it. On `[1, 0, 1, 0, 1]` with $K = 2$ the seeded sweep returns $4$; the unseeded one returns $2$ — exactly the two windows that start at index $0$ (@sec-cnt-a4's `fig-cnt-a4`, where the two cyan lookups are the seed being read).
- **Using $\text{atMost}(K) - \text{atMost}(K-1)$ on an array with negatives.** The rung rests on "if `a[left..right]` is legal, every shorter suffix of it is too", which a negative entry breaks. On `[1,-1,1,-1,1]` with $K = 0$ the difference answers $10$, the honest "at most $0$" count is $9$, and "exactly $0$" is $6$ — three different numbers, none of them right twice. Use the prefix hash (@sec-cnt-a4, @sec-cnt-p3-binsum).
- **Breaking ties in the same direction on both sides of a span count.** Pop `<=` left and `<` right (or the exact mirror) and the credits partition the windows. Pop `<=` on both and `[3, 3]` is credited $[2, 2]$ — four claims for three windows, sum of maxima $12$ against a true $9$; on `[1, 3, 3]` the credits are $[1, 4, 3]$ and the answer is $22$ instead of $16$. Pop `<` on both and `[1, 3, 3]` shrinks to $[1, 2, 1]$, answering $10$. The diagnostic is cheap: **each credit row must sum to $\binom{n+1}{2}$** (@sec-cnt-a2, @sec-cnt-p1-ranges).
- **Reading the cover-sum as a window count.** $\sum_i (i+1)(n-i) = \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}$, which at $n = 4$ is $20$ — the *sum of window lengths*, not the $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ windows. Likewise $\sum_i \lceil (i+1)(n-i)/2 \rceil = 10$ at $n = 4$ is the sum of odd window *lengths*, while the *number* of odd windows is $6$, from cut-point parity (@sec-cnt-a1).
- **Closing a histogram for a relation that is not an equivalence.** $\sum_c \binom{c}{2}$ counts unordered *same-class* pairs. On inversions ($a_i > a_j$ with $i < j$) the classes are not a partition at all: for `[3, 1, 2, 1]` the value histogram is $\{3:1, 1:2, 2:1\}$, whose $\sum \binom{c}{2} = 1$ is supposed to stand in for $4$ inversions. Order-sensitive conditions need the fix-one-end sweep, with a Fenwick tree once $n$ is large (@sec-cnt-a3).
- **Counting inversions with the pair sweep at $n = 10^5$.** "Fix the right end" is $O(n)$ only when the complement is a single key. Inversions need a prefix-count over values, which is @sec-lts-a5's table or a tree — and the count is $\binom{n}{2}$, which is where the next bullet bites.
- **An `int` accumulator.** Pair counts and window counts reach $\binom{n}{2}$: @sec-cnt-p1-oddsum's constraints ($n \le 100$, $arr[i] \le 1000$) cap the answer at $1000 \cdot \frac{100 \cdot 101 \cdot 102}{6} = 171{,}700{,}000$, an `int`; @sec-cnt-p2-songs at $n = 6 \cdot 10^4$ can report $\binom{60000}{2} = 1{,}799{,}970{,}000$, which fits with only $347{,}513{,}647$ to spare; @sec-cnt-p1-ranges at $n = 1000$ and $|v| \le 10^9$ reaches $500{,}500 \cdot 10^9 \approx 5 \cdot 10^{14}$ for the maxima alone, and @sec-cnt-p3-ones at $n = 10^5$ reaches $5{,}000{,}050{,}000$ — more than four times $2^{31}$, which is why its statement hands you a modulus (@sec-cnt-a3, @sec-arr-size-trap).
- **A raw `s % k` in C++ or Java on a negative prefix.** `(-2) % 5` is $-2$, not $3$, so residue buckets split into mirror images and the count comes out low. Normalise with `((s % k) + k) % k`; Python's `%` already returns a non-negative residue, which is why the same bug is invisible in the Python tab (@sec-cnt-a4, @sec-pref-p2-b).
- **An unclamped value interval.** With $lo = \max(a_j - a, a_k - c)$ and $hi = \min(a_j + a, a_k + c)$, nothing forces $0 \le lo$ or $hi \le V$: the clamped `lo = max(0, ...)` / `hi = min(V, ...)` is what stops a negative index (which in *Python* silently wraps and reads the wrong end of the table) and an out-of-range read. And if $lo > hi$ the interval is empty — `cum[hi + 1] - cum[lo]` then returns a *negative* charge. @sec-cnt-p4-triplets shows both failures as runnable asserts (@sec-cnt-a5).
- **"Count the valid $(i,j)$ pairs, count the valid $(j,k)$ pairs, multiply."** When the three conditions form a triangle rather than a chain, the closing condition couples the halves. On @sec-cnt-p4-triplets' first sample that shortcut answers $5$ instead of $4$; the intruder is $(0,4,5) = (3,9,7)$, where $|3-9| = 6 \le a$ and $|9-7| = 2 \le b$ hold but $|3-7| = 4 > c$. Keep the pivot and query the interval instead (@sec-cnt-a5).
- **Reading $i < j \le k$ as $i < j < k$.** @sec-cnt-p4-xortri's $j$ may sit *on* $k$, because then $b$ is the single element $arr[k]$; on the first sample two of the four triplets are of that shape, charging each zero-XOR window $k - i$ (the right count of split points) gives $4$, while $k - i - 1$, or counting windows instead of split points, gives $2$ (@sec-cnt-p4-xortri).
- **Judging a frequency bucket while its value is still moving.** In a counter of counters, `how[f]` only becomes meaningful once no future increment can change the letter that produced it. Move `maxf`/`minf` lazily, clamp them to the live range, and never read a bucket for a letter whose count is still being written in the same step (@sec-cnt-p5-beauty, @sec-ds).
- **Rank weights on an unsorted list.** $\sum_k b_k(2k - n + 1)$ is the sum of pairwise distances only when $b$ is sorted; on `[8, 1, 4, 3]` as given it returns $-12$ instead of $22$ (@sec-cnt-pairsum).
- **One key for an asymmetric index condition.** $j - i = a_i + a_j$ pairs the key $i + a_i$ of the *left* member with the key $j - a_j$ of the *right* member; grouping by either key alone and adding $\binom{c}{2}$ counts a different relation (@sec-cnt-idxval, @sec-cnt-pidx-message).
- **Subtracting two overlapping bad sets without adding back.** "Contains $x$ and $y$" is all windows minus no-$x$ minus no-$y$ **plus** neither; drop the last term and every window with neither value is subtracted twice. On `[1, 2, 1, 3, 2]` the right answer is $8$ (@sec-cnt-comp).
- **Multiplying left and right counts when the ends are coupled.** The product $\text{left}_j \cdot \text{right}_j$ is exact only when no condition links $i$ and $k$ (@sec-cnt-p4-teams); with one (@sec-cnt-p4-triplets) it overcounts.
:::

## Exercises

**1. [E] For $n = 5$ write out the cover counts $(i+1)(n-i)$. What is their sum, how many subarrays are there, and what do the two numbers mean?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[5, 8, 9, 8, 5]$, summing to $35 = \frac{5 \cdot 6 \cdot 7}{6}$. There are $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ subarrays. The $35$ is the cover sum — each window counted once *per element it contains*, i.e. the sum of window lengths — so it is not a check on your arithmetic; the $15$ is the window count (@sec-cnt-a1).
:::

**2. [E] For $n = 5$ give the odd-length cover counts and their sum, then count the odd-length windows two different ways.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\lceil (i+1)(n-i)/2 \rceil = [3, 4, 5, 4, 3]$, sum $19$, which is the *sum of the odd window lengths*. The number of odd-length windows comes from cut-point parity: among $0 .. 5$ there are $3$ even and $3$ odd cuts, so $3 \times 3 = 9$ odd windows and $\binom{3}{2} + \binom{3}{2} = 6$ even ones — $15$ in total (@sec-cnt-a1).
:::

**3. [E] For `nums = [2, 1, 2]` list the six subarrays and their maxima, then compute the max-credits under the canonical rule (pop `<=` left, `<` right) and under both same-predicate variants. Which rows actually partition the windows?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The six maxima are $[2]=2$, $[1]=1$, $[2]=2$, $[2,1]=2$, $[1,2]=2$, $[2,1,2]=2$, so $\sum \max = 11$. Canonical: $L = [1, 1, 3]$, $R = [2, 1, 1]$, credits $[2, 1, 3]$ — they sum to $6 = \binom{4}{2}$ and weight to $2\cdot2 + 1\cdot1 + 2\cdot3 = 11$ ✓. Both passes popping `<=`: credits $[3, 1, 3]$ — seven claims for six windows, total $13$. Both passes popping `<`: credits $[2, 1, 2]$ — five claims, total $9$. The middle slot's credit is $1$ in all three rows; the disagreement is entirely about the window `[2, 1, 2]`, whose maximum appears twice: popping `<=` on both sides lets both `2`s claim it, popping `<` on both sides lets neither claim it (@sec-cnt-a2).
:::

**4. [E] On `nums = [1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 3]` give the charge `seen[v]` collected at each index, the final histogram, and the two totals. Why do both work here?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Charges $[0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 1]$ sum to $4$. The histogram is $\{1: 3, 2: 1, 3: 2\}$, and $\binom{3}{2} + \binom{1}{2} + \binom{2}{2} = 3 + 0 + 1 = 4$. Both work because "equal values" is an equivalence relation with no direction to respect; the sweep is the one that survives when the relation stops being symmetric (@sec-cnt-a3, @sec-cnt-p2-goodpairs).
:::

**5. [E] Run the seeded prefix sweep on (a) `[1, 1, 1, 1]` with $K = 2$ and (b) `[0, 0, 0]` with $K = 0$. Then delete the `cnt[0] = 1` seed and re-run on `[1, 0, 1, 0, 1]` with $K = 2$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $3$ (the three length-two windows). (b) $6$ — every window, since all $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ of them sum to $0$; zeros are the worst case for a map keyed by prefix value, because the prefix never moves and all four cut points share one key. (c) With the seed $4$; without it $2$. The two that vanish are `[1,0,1]` and `[1,0,1,0]`, the windows whose left end is the *empty* prefix — the entry `cnt[0] = 1` is the only thing that can report them (@sec-cnt-a4).
:::

**6. [E] For `a = [1, -1, 1, -1, 1]` report the number of windows with sum exactly $0$, the number with sum at most $0$, the number with sum at least $1$, and $\binom{6}{2}$. What does $\text{atMost}(0) - \text{atMost}(-1)$ give?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Exactly $0$: $6$. At most $0$: $9$. At least $1$: $15 - 9 = 6$ by complement, and the total is $\binom{6}{2} = 15$. The sliding-window rung reports `atMost(0) = 10` (its shrink loop books four windows at `right = 4`, two of which — `a[2..4]` and `a[4..4]` — have sum $1$), and `atMost(-1) = 0`, so the difference claims there are $10$ windows with sum exactly $0$ when there are $6$ — an over-count of $4$ that comes entirely from the non-monotone shrink loop (@sec-cnt-a4).
:::

**7. [E] Count the windows of `[4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1]` whose sum is divisible by $5$ two ways: the seeded residue sweep and the $\sum \binom{c}{2}$ closure over residue classes. Why does the second one work even though the array has negatives?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both give $7$. The residue sweep keys on `p % k` and adds `cnt[r]`; the closure buckets the six prefix residues and adds $\binom{c}{2}$ per bucket. They agree because "same residue" *is* an equivalence relation — the ordering-sensitive part lives entirely in "the earlier prefix is a left end", which $\binom{c}{2}$ handles by choosing two cut points from one class. The C++ versions must normalise with `((s % k) + k) % k` (@sec-cnt-a4, @sec-pref-p2-b).
:::

**8. [E] How many subarrays of `[11, 21, 35, 77]` have an odd sum? Do it by parity buckets rather than by looping, and say which invariant makes that legal.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The prefix parities over the five cut points $0..4$ are $[0, 1, 0, 1, 0]$: three even, two odd. A window is odd exactly when its two cuts differ in parity, giving $3 \times 2 = 6$ windows, which matches the brute count. The invariant is that only the *parity of the prefix* is used, so $11$ and $21$ are interchangeable — the same cut-parity argument as the odd-length window count in @sec-cnt-a1, but keyed on value parity instead of index parity (@sec-cnt-a4, [LC 1524 · Number of Sub-arrays With Odd Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-sub-arrays-with-odd-sum/){difficulty="Medium"}).
:::

**9. [M] Exactly $k$ odd numbers, from two rungs. For `nums = [1, 1, 1, 1]` and $k = 2$ report $\text{atMost}(2)$, $\text{atMost}(1)$ and the difference. Do the same for `[1, 0, 1, 0, 1]` with $k = 1$ and for `[2, 4, 6]` with $k = 2$. What do the zeros contribute, and what would $\text{exactly}(0)$ require?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`[1,1,1,1]`: $\text{atMost}(2) = 7$ (the four singletons plus the three length-two windows), $\text{atMost}(1) = 4$, difference $3$ — and the three are exactly the windows `[0..1]`, `[1..2]`, `[2..3]`. `[1,0,1,0,1]`: $\text{atMost}(1) = 10$, $\text{atMost}(0) = 2$ (the two single-`0` windows), so $\text{exactly}(1) = 8$ out of $\binom{6}{2} = 15$. `[2,4,6]`: $\text{atMost}(2) = \text{atMost}(1) = 6$, difference $0$ — the rung reports an impossible target without a special case. Zeros are what make $\text{atMost}(0)$ non-zero, and $\text{exactly}(0)$ needs the convention $\text{atMost}(-1) = 0$ (@sec-cnt-a4, @sec-cnt-p3-binsum, [LC 1248 · Count Number of Nice Subarrays](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-number-of-nice-subarrays/){difficulty="Medium"}).
:::

**10. [E] Two credit rows, one answer. You already have $\sum \max = 11$ for `[2, 1, 2]`. Compute $\sum \min$ and the sum of ranges. Then give the closed forms of both rows for a *strictly increasing* array and check them on `[1, 2, 3]`**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Minima $8$, ranges $11 - 8 = 3$ — which is the direct list ($0$ for each singleton, $1$ for each of the three longer windows). On a strictly increasing array the maximum of a window is always its **last** element, so slot $k$ wins the $k+1$ windows that end at it: $\sum \max = \sum_k a_k (k+1) = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14$. The minimum is always its **first** element, so slot $j$ wins the $n-j$ windows that start there: $\sum \min = \sum_j a_j (n - j) = 3 + 4 + 3 = 10$. Difference $4$, which is LC 2104's first-sample answer (@sec-cnt-a2, @sec-cnt-p1-ranges).
:::

**11. [M] Which condition are you allowed to drop? On `arr = [3, 0, 1, 1, 9, 7]`, $a = 7$, $b = 2$, $c = 3$, count the triples satisfying only the two *adjacent* conditions $|arr_i - arr_j| \le a$ and $|arr_j - arr_k| \le b$. Which extra triple appears, and what does the fixed-middle loop compute instead**?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Five instead of four. The intruder is $(0,4,5) = (3,9,7)$: $|3 - 9| = 6 \le 7$ and $|9 - 7| = 2 \le 2$ both hold, while the closing condition fails with $|3 - 7| = 4 > 3$. The pivot never multiplies two independent counts: at $j = 4$ the only admissible $k$ is $5$ and the value interval is $[\max(9-7, 7-3),\ \min(9+7, 7+3)] = [4, 10]$, which holds none of the left multiset $\{3, 0, 1, 1\}$, so the charge is $0$ (@sec-cnt-a5, @sec-cnt-p4-triplets).
:::

**12. [M] Charges and costs. Reproduce the charge-by-middle-index table for `arr = [3, 0, 1, 1, 9, 7]`, count the primitive steps each rung takes at $n = 6$ with $V = 1000$, and say where the fixed-middle rung overtakes the triple loop for $V = 1000$, $V = 500$ and $V = 26$**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Charges $j = 1 \to 2$, $j = 2 \to 2$, $j = 3 \to 0$, $j = 4 \to 0$, totalling $4$. Rung 1 touches $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ triples; rung 2 rebuilds a $V + 2 = 1002$-cell cumulative table once per middle index — $(n-2)(V+2) + \binom{n-1}{2}$-ish pair work $= 4018$ steps, about $200$ times as many. The table rebuild is the whole cost, so the crossover is a statement about $V$ as much as $n$: the first $n$ where the rung wins is $80$ at $V = 1000$ ($81{,}237 < 82{,}160$), $57$ at $V = 500$, and $16$ once $V$ is alphabet-sized at $26$. Rebuilding the table *only when a value enters it* is what turns $O(nV)$ into $O(n^2)$ or better (@sec-cnt-a5).
:::

**13. [M] Cut points, windows and a free index. For `arr = [2, 3, 1, 6, 7]` write the prefix-XOR array, list the pairs of equal prefixes, and turn each pair into triplets $(i, j, k)$ with $i < j \le k$. What goes wrong if you charge $k - i - 1$, or if you insist on $j < k$**?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`px = [0, 2, 1, 0, 6, 1]`, so the equal-prefix cut pairs are $(0, 3)$ and $(2, 5)$ — the zero-XOR windows $(0, 2)$ and $(2, 4)$. For a window $(i, k)$ the split point $j$ may be any of $i+1 .. k$, i.e. $k - i$ choices, so each window is worth $2$ and the total is $4$: $(0,1,2), (0,2,2), (2,3,4), (2,4,4)$. Charging $k - i - 1$ counts only the *strictly interior* cut points and returns $2$; forbidding $j = k$ deletes the two triplets whose second array is the single element $arr[k]$ — also $2$, and counting windows instead of triplets gives $2$ for the same reason. On `[1, 1, 1, 1, 1]` the correct sweep returns $10$ (@sec-cnt-p4-xortri).
:::

**14. [E] Reading a count table. Which of these arrays have a lucky value ($\mathrm{cnt}[v] = v$, report the largest): `[1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]`, `[2, 2, 3, 3, 3]`, `[2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 1, 1]`, `[2, 2, 2]`, `[7, 7, 7]`, `[1]`, `[5, 5, 5]`? Bound the number of lucky values when $n = 500$**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$3$, $3$, $3$, $-1$, $-1$, $1$, $-1$. In `[2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 1, 1]` all three values are candidates and two pass ($\mathrm{cnt}[2] = 2$, $\mathrm{cnt}[3] = 3$) while $\mathrm{cnt}[1] = 2$ misses by one; `[5, 5, 5]` has $\mathrm{cnt}[5] = 3$, so a value larger than $n$ can never be lucky. A lucky $v$ occupies $v$ slots, so the lucky values consume $\sum_v v^2$ cells of an $n$-cell array: $1^2 + \cdots + 10^2 = 385 \le 500 < 506 = 1^2 + \cdots + 11^2$, so at most $10$ of the $501$ table cells can pass the test (@sec-cnt-a5, @sec-cnt-p5-lucky).
:::

**15. [E] Which buckets pair with themselves? For `times = [30, 20, 150, 100, 40]` list the residues mod $60$ and build the pair count from cross-class products plus $\binom{c}{2}$ inside self-pairing classes. Which residues self-pair, and how does the one-pass sweep dodge the taxonomy?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Residues $[30, 20, 30, 40, 40]$. Cross: the one `20` with the two `40`s gives $1 \times 2 = 2$; inside: the two `30`s give $\binom{2}{2} = 1$; residue `0` is empty, contributing $\binom{0}{2} = 0$. Total $3$, which is the brute count. Self-pairing residues are those with $2r \equiv 0$, i.e. $r = 0$ and $r = k/2 = 30$ — they take $\binom{c}{2}$, never $c^2$. The sweep never classifies anything: it adds `cnt[(60 - r) % 60]` *before* inserting the current song, so a `30` can only ever be charged against earlier `30`s (@sec-cnt-p2-songs).
:::

**16. [E] A key is a design decision. For `dominoes = [(1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 2), (1, 3)]` count the equivalent pairs by brute force and then by a histogram over the key $\min \cdot 10 + \max$. What has to change if faces can reach $500$, and does the answer size worry you?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Brute force finds $3$ pairs; the histogram is $\{12: 3, 13: 1\}$, closing to $\binom{3}{2} + \binom{1}{2} = 3$. Reversal makes $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$ one class, so this is an equivalence relation — no order to respect, no sweep needed (@sec-cnt-a3). The mixed-radix key needs a base strictly above the largest face: $10$ is legal only while faces are $\le 9$, which is exactly the stated constraint; at $500$ you need $\min \cdot 501 + \max \le 251{,}000$ (fine as an array index or a `long long`) or a tuple key in a hash map. At $n \le 4 \cdot 10^4$ the count tops out at $\binom{40000}{2} = 799{,}980{,}000$ — still a signed `int`, with room to spare (@sec-cnt-p5-lucky's table-vs-map choice is the same decision, [LC 1128 · Number of Equivalent Domino Pairs](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-equivalent-domino-pairs/){difficulty="Easy"}).
:::

**17. [M] Rounding up to a group size. How many rabbits are in the forest when `answers = [1, 1, 2]`, `[1, 1, 1]`, `[2, 2, 2, 2, 2]`, `[10]`, `[0, 0, 0]`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sum_x \lceil n_x / (x+1) \rceil \cdot (x+1)$ gives $5$, $4$, $6$, $11$ and $3$. A rabbit answering $x$ is claiming a group of $x+1$ rabbits, so $n_x$ reporters fill $\lceil n_x/(x+1) \rceil$ whole groups; $[1,1,2] = \lceil 2/2 \rceil \cdot 2 + \lceil 1/3 \rceil \cdot 3 = 2 + 3$. Note the shape of the reasoning: the answer is not the number of *rabbits observed* but the number implied by rounding a *count-table entry* up to a capacity — a counter-of-counters one level below @sec-cnt-p5-beauty and @sec-ds ([LC 781 · Rabbits in Forest](https://leetcode.com/problems/rabbits-in-forest/){difficulty="Medium"}).
:::

**18. [M] One string, three questions. For `s = "0110111"` give (a) the number of substrings, (b) the number made only of `1`s, and (c) the number containing at most one `0`**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\binom{8}{2} = 28$. (b) $9$: the stream charges $[0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3]$ (the length of the `1`-run ending at each position), and the runs $[0, 2, 3]$ give $\binom{1}{2} + \binom{3}{2} + \binom{4}{2} = 0 + 3 + 6$. (c) $24 = 9 + 15$, where the fifteen single-zero substrings come from each `0` at $p$ with its neighbouring zeros at $\ell$ and $r$ worth $(p - \ell)(r - p)$: the `0` at index $0$ gives $1 \times 3 = 3$ and the one at index $3$ gives $3 \times 4 = 12$. (b) counts a run, (c) counts *around* the zeros — complementary counting in the sense of @sec-cnt-p3-ones, and if the question had been "longest run after flipping at most one `0`" you would be in [LC 1004 · Max Consecutive Ones III](https://leetcode.com/problems/max-consecutive-ones-iii/){difficulty="Medium"}, the optimisation twin of the same statistic.
:::

**19. [M] A bucket table read too early. Recompute the beauty sum for `"aaab"`, `"aaabbb"` and `"abc"`, then evaluate the common slip of using $\max_f - 1$ in place of $\max_f - \min_f$ on each and on `"aabcb"`**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The correct answers are $3$, $8$, $0$ and $5$. The slip gives $6$ on `"aabcb"` and $0$ on `"abc"` — i.e. it is *invisible* on a string whose letters are all distinct, because there $\max_f = \min_f = 1$ and $\max_f - 1$ happens to agree. $\min_f$ is the minimum over letters *present in the window*, so it has to come from a table that is touched when a letter arrives for the first time, and the cursor for $\min_f$ may only move while the bucket it leaves is provably empty (@sec-cnt-p5-beauty, @sec-ds).
:::

**20. [H] Name the pattern, then the rung. Classify each statement and give the complexity of the best answer: (i) "sum of $\max$ over all subarrays"; (ii) "count subarrays with sum exactly $K$, values may be negative"; (iii) "count pairs $i < j$ with $\mathrm{nums}[i] > \mathrm{nums}[j]$"; (iv) "count triples with $|a_i - a_j| \le a$, $|a_j - a_k| \le b$, $|a_i - a_k| \le c$"; (v) "count subarrays whose set of values equals the set of the whole array, $n \le 1000$"**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(i) Credit the winner: two monotonic-stack passes with opposite tie-breaking, $O(n)$ (@sec-cnt-a2, @sec-cnt-p1-ranges). (ii) Prefix equality in a hash map seeded with `cnt[0] = 1`, $O(n)$ — the $\text{atMost}$ difference is forbidden (@sec-cnt-a4, [LC 560 · Subarray Sum Equals K](https://leetcode.com/problems/subarray-sum-equals-k/){difficulty="Medium"}). (iii) An order-sensitive relation: fix the right end and ask a structure how many earlier values are larger — $O(n + V)$ with @sec-lts-a5's table when $V$ is small, otherwise $O(n \log n)$ with @sec-salgo-a3's merge (or a Fenwick tree, a later volume); $\sum \binom{c}{2}$ is simply wrong here (@sec-cnt-a3, [LC 2537 · Count the Number of Good Subarrays](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-the-number-of-good-subarrays/){difficulty="Medium"} for the same shape with a threshold). (iv) Fix the middle and answer one interval query on a value histogram, $O(nV + n^2)$ — and at $n \le 100$, $V \le 1000$ the plain triple loop is $161{,}700$ steps, which is also fine (@sec-cnt-p4-triplets). (v) Enumerate the left end and extend a `seen` map until every distinct value has appeared: $O(n^2)$ with $n \le 1000$ is $10^6$ steps, so the naive loop *is* the answer — recognising when a double loop is affordable is half of @sec-cnt-why ([LC 2799 · Count Complete Subarrays in an Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-complete-subarrays-in-an-array/){difficulty="Medium"}).
:::

**21. [E] For `a = [1, 2, 3, 4]` compute $\sum_{i<j} a_i a_j$ and $\sum_{i<j} (a_i + a_j)$ without listing pairs.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sum a = 10$ and $\sum a^2 = 30$, so $\sum_{i<j} a_i a_j = (100 - 30)/2 = 35$ — the six products $2 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 12$. Each element has $n - 1 = 3$ partners, so $\sum_{i<j}(a_i + a_j) = 3 \cdot 10 = 30$. Both are @eq-cnt-swap with "pairs containing $a_i$" as the set (@sec-cnt-pairsum).
:::

**22. [M] For `a = [1, 2, 3]` compute the sums of $a_i \oplus a_j$, $a_i \,\&\, a_j$ and $a_i \mid a_j$ over all pairs, bit by bit.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Bit 0 is set in $1$ and $3$ ($c_0 = 2$), bit 1 in $2$ and $3$ ($c_1 = 2$), $n = 3$. XOR: $c(n-c) = 2$ pairs per bit, so $2 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 = 6$. AND: $\binom{2}{2} = 1$ pair per bit, so $1 + 2 = 3$. OR: $\binom{3}{2} - \binom{1}{2} = 3$ pairs per bit, so $3 + 6 = 9$. Directly: XORs $3, 2, 1$; ANDs $0, 1, 2$; ORs $3, 3, 3$ (@sec-cnt-pairsum).
:::

**23. [M] Count the pairs $i < j$ with $j - i = a_i + a_j$ in `a = [1, 1, 1, 1]` (0-based indices) with the two-key sweep, and explain why grouping by $i + a_i$ alone fails.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Left keys $i + a_i = [1, 2, 3, 4]$, right keys $j - a_j = [-1, 0, 1, 2]$. At $j = 2$ the right key $1$ meets the left key of $i = 0$; at $j = 3$ the right key $2$ meets $i = 1$: two pairs, $(0, 2)$ and $(1, 3)$, both with $j - i = 2 = 1 + 1$. Grouping by $i + a_i$ finds no repeated key at all and answers $0$, because the condition compares a left key with a *right* key, which is a different function of the index (@sec-cnt-idxval).
:::

**24. [M] How many windows of `[1, 2, 1, 3, 2]` contain both a `1` and a `2`? Use inclusion–exclusion.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
All windows: $\binom{6}{2} = 15$. Without a `1`: the runs `[2]` and `[3, 2]` hold $1 + 3 = 4$. Without a `2`: the runs `[1]` and `[1, 3]` hold $1 + 3 = 4$. Without either: the run `[3]` holds $1$. So $15 - 4 - 4 + 1 = 8$. Forgetting the $+1$ answers $7$: the window `[3]` was removed twice (@sec-cnt-comp).
:::

**25. [M] Count pairs $i < j$ with $a_i = a_j$ and $j - i \ge 2$ in `[1, 2, 1, 1, 2]` with one sweep. Where does the index condition go?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Into the insertion order: when the cursor is at $j$, insert $a_{j-2}$ first, so the table holds exactly the indices at distance at least $2$. The sweep finds $(0, 2)$ at $j = 2$, $(0, 3)$ at $j = 3$ (index $2$ is not yet eligible) and $(1, 4)$ at $j = 4$: $3$ pairs. The pair $(2, 3)$ is excluded because index $2$ enters the table only at $j = 4$ (@sec-cnt-idxval).
:::

**26. [H] Ball in Berland, but couples may repeat: $(1,1), (1,1), (2,2)$. Count pairs of couples with no common person.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\binom{3}{2} = 3$ pairs. Same boy: boy $1$ has degree $2$, one pair. Same girl: girl $1$ has degree $2$, one pair. Both: the two identical couples share both, one pair, and inclusion–exclusion adds it back: $3 - 1 - 1 + 1 = 2$. The good pairs are the two that use couple $(2,2)$. With distinct couples the last term is $0$, which is why the problem as stated needs no add-back (@sec-cnt-pcomp-ball).
:::

## Interview questions

**1. How do you compute the sum of the sums of every subarray in one pass, and why is the formula right?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Do not enumerate windows; ask how many of them contain slot $i$. A window is a pair of cut points with the left one in $\{0..i\}$ and the right one in $\{i..n-1\}$, so $i$ is covered $(i+1)(n-i)$ times and the answer is $\sum_i a_i (i+1)(n-i)$. Sanity-check by putting $a_i = 1$: the cover sum must be $\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}$, the *sum of window lengths* — $20$ at $n = 4$, against $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ windows. Both numbers come out of the same formula, and naming the difference is what separates a derivation from a recitation (@sec-cnt-a1).
:::

**2. How does that answer change if only odd-length subarrays count?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Nothing about the swap changes; only the cover count does. Of the $(i+1)(n-i)$ windows covering slot $i$, half have odd length, and when that product is odd the odd class is the larger one, so it is $\lceil (i+1)(n-i)/2 \rceil$. At $n = 5$ the odd covers are $[3, 4, 5, 4, 3]$ and the answer for `[1,4,2,5,3]` is $3 + 16 + 10 + 20 + 9 = 58$. Watch for the trap in the follow-up: "and how many odd-length windows are there?" is *not* $19$ — it is $(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1) \lceil n/2 \rceil$, i.e. $3 \times 3 = 9$ at $n = 5$ and $3 \times 2 = 6$ at $n = 4$, counted by choosing cut points of opposite parity (@sec-cnt-a1, @sec-cnt-p1-oddsum).
:::

**3. Why do cover counts fail for the sum of $\max - \min$ over all subarrays, and what replaces them?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A maximum is not additive, so the credit has to be re-derived as "the windows in which this slot is the *appointed* winner", and the appointment has to be unique. Each slot's span is a product $L_i R_i$ of two distances found by a monotonic stack, and the tie-break must be strict on one side and non-strict on the other — pop `<=` going left, `<` going right (or the mirror). Then $\sum \max - \min = \sum_i a_i (L_i R_i - L'_i R'_i)$ in $O(n)$. Prove you know the failure mode: on `[3, 3]` with the same predicate on both passes the credits are $[2,2]$ — four claims for three windows — and the sum of maxima comes out $12$ instead of $9$. The cheap invariant is that each credit row must sum to $\binom{n+1}{2}$ (@sec-cnt-a2, @sec-cnt-p1-ranges).
:::

**4. Can a sliding window count the subarrays that sum to $K$ when the array has negatives?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. A shrink loop is a monotonicity argument — "if `a[left..right]` is legal, every shorter suffix is too" — and a negative entry breaks it. On `[1,-1,1,-1,1]` with $K = 0$ the window rung answers $10$, the honest at-most-$0$ count is $9$, and the true exactly-$0$ count is $6$. Use prefix equality: $P[r] - P[l] = K$, so sweep the right end and add `cnt[p - K]` before inserting `cnt[p]`, seeded with `cnt[0] = 1`. $O(n)$ on any integers, and the seed is what lets a window start at index $0$ (@sec-cnt-a4, @sec-pref-p2-a).
:::

**5. How do you count subarrays whose sum is divisible by $k$, and why might a C++ version disagree with Python?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Same sweep, keyed on the *residue*: $P[r] \equiv P[l] \pmod k$, so add `cnt[p]` then `cnt[p] += 1` with `p = ((s % k) + k) % k`. In C++ and Java `(-2) % 5` is $-2$, not $3$, so unnormalised keys split each bucket into two mirror images and the count comes out low; Python's `%` is already non-negative, which is why the bug is invisible there. Equivalent offline statement: bucket the $n+1$ prefix residues and add $\binom{c}{2}$ per bucket — that form works even with negatives because "same residue" is an equivalence relation (@sec-cnt-a4, @sec-pref-p2-b, cross-checked on `[4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1]` with $k = 5$, which gives $7$ both ways).
:::

**6. When do you reach for $\text{atMost}(k) - \text{atMost}(k-1)$ to count windows with exactly $k$ of something?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When the window statistic is monotone under shrinking, which for sums means non-negative entries — binary arrays, counts of odds, lengths. Then two calls to one shrinking loop give $O(n)$, with $\text{atMost}(-1) = 0$ as the base case. On `[1,1,1,1]` with $k = 2$ that is $7 - 4 = 3$; on `[1,0,1,0,1]` with $k = 1$, $10 - 2 = 8$. With negatives the identity is false (@sec-cnt-a4). The other reflex to state: $\text{exactly}$ of a *shape* property (all `1`s) is a run decomposition, not a difference of two rungs (@sec-cnt-p3-ones).
:::

**7. What are the two ways to count equal-value pairs, and which one generalises to inversions?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Fix the right end and add `seen[v]`, or build the histogram once and add $\binom{c}{2}$ — on `[1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 3]` both give $4$ (charges $[0,0,0,1,2,1]$, and $\binom{3}{2} + \binom{1}{2} + \binom{2}{2}$). Only the first generalises, because $\sum \binom{c}{2}$ presumes the relation is an equivalence: for inversions on `[3, 1, 2, 1]` the histogram answers $1$ where there are $4$ inversions. When $i < j$ and $a_i > a_j$ matter, "how many earlier values are bigger?" is a prefix query over *values* — a table if the range is small, otherwise merge sort or a Fenwick tree (@sec-cnt-a3, @sec-lts-a5, @sec-salgo-a3).
:::

**8. How do you count triples $(i, j, k)$ with three pairwise value conditions when $n \le 100$ and $arr[i] \le 1000$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Start with the triple loop ($\binom{100}{3} = 161{,}700$ steps — say out loud that it is affordable), then improve it by pivoting on $j$: with $j$ fixed, the condition on $i$ and the condition on $k$ are independent, and "$|a_i - a_j| \le a$ and $|a_i - a_k| \le c$" is one interval $[\max(a_j - a, a_k - c), \min(a_j + a, a_k + c)]$ clamped to $[0, V]$, answered by a subtraction on a cumulative histogram. $O(nV + n^2)$. Two traps to volunteer: clamping (an unclamped negative index reads the wrong end of the table in Python and is undefined behaviour in C++), and not multiplying the two pair counts — on `[3, 0, 1, 1, 9, 7]`, $a = 7, b = 2, c = 3$ the product method gives $5$ because $(0,4,5) = (3,9,7)$ passes the two chain conditions and fails $|3 - 7| \le 3$ (@sec-cnt-a5, @sec-cnt-p4-triplets).
:::

**9. When counting triplets whose left-part XOR equals their right-part XOR, why does the middle index disappear?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Because $x \oplus x = 0$: writing $a = P[j] \oplus P[i]$ and $b = P[k+1] \oplus P[j]$ (with $P$ the prefix XOR), $a = b$ iff $P[i] = P[k+1]$, and $P[j]$ cancels. So count equal-prefix cut pairs — windows $(i, k)$ with $P[i] = P[k+1]$ — and then remember that every $j \in \{i+1..k\}$ is a legal split, which is $k - i$ triplets, not $k - i - 1$. On `[2, 3, 1, 6, 7]`: $P = [0, 2, 1, 0, 6, 1]$, windows $(0,2)$ and $(2,4)$, each worth $2$, total $4$. Dropping the $j = k$ case (a single-element right array) gives $2$ (@sec-cnt-p4-xortri).
:::

**10. Before writing an $O(n)$ counting solution, how do you choose the accumulator type and decide whether the answer needs a modulus?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Estimate the answer first. $\binom{60000}{2} = 1{,}799{,}970{,}000$ fits a signed 32-bit int with $347{,}513{,}647$ left over; $\binom{10^5}{2} = 4{,}999{,}950{,}000$ does not, and LC 1513's answer $5{,}000{,}050{,}000$ (all-`1` string at $n = 10^5$) is why that statement hands you $10^9 + 7$. Mixed products are worse: LC 2104 at $n = 1000$ with $|v| \le 10^9$ reaches about $5 \cdot 10^{14}$ for the maxima alone, so the *credit* must be 64-bit even though $n$ is small. Accumulate in `long long`, reduce only at the end (or after each addition, never before) (@sec-cnt-a3, @sec-arr-size-trap).
:::

**11. What does a constraint like $1 \le arr[i] \le 500$ buy you?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
An array indexed by *value*: $501$ cells, $O(1)$ lookups, no hashing, no sorting. Conditions like $\mathrm{cnt}[v] = v$ (@sec-cnt-p5-lucky) or "$|a_i - a_j| \le a$" (@sec-cnt-a5) become table reads, and the same trick gives a bound for free: a lucky $v$ occupies $v$ slots, so lucky values cost $\sum v^2 \le n$ — at $n = 500$ at most $10$ of them, since $1^2 + \cdots + 10^2 = 385 \le 500 < 506$. Alphabet-size constraints ($26$ letters, $\le 100$ values) are the same gift. The failure mode is solving it with maps and sorts when the statement offered an address (@sec-lts-a5).
:::

**12. For the sum of beauty (max frequency minus min frequency) over all substrings, how do you improve an $O(n^2 \cdot 26)$ solution's inner step?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The outer $O(n^2)$ is the enumeration; the win is making each extension $O(1)$. Keep `cnt[letter]` *and* `how[f]` — a counter of counters — so the extremes are cursors over frequency buckets instead of a scan of $26$ cells. The hard part is the discipline: $\min_f$ is over letters *present* in the window, so a bucket only becomes meaningful once a letter's first arrival has been recorded, and a cursor may move only while the bucket it is leaving is provably empty. Two sample values to keep: `"aabcb"` $= 5$ over $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ windows, `"aaabbb"` $= 8$. And the trap: using $\max_f - 1$ gives $6$ instead of $5$ on `"aabcb"` and no error at all on `"abc"`, so a sample can hide it completely (@sec-cnt-p5-beauty, @sec-ds).
:::

**13. Rabbits report how many others share their colour; what is the smallest population consistent with the reports?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Group by the answer: $n_x$ rabbits reporting $x$ must be split into groups of size $x+1$, so they imply $\lceil n_x / (x+1) \rceil \cdot (x+1)$ rabbits. On `[1,1,2]` that is $2 + 3 = 5$; `[1,1,1]` is $4$ (one group of two, one rabbit short of a third pair), `[2,2,2,2,2]` is $6$, `[10]` is $11$, `[0,0,0]` is $3$. Pedagogically it is the same move as this chapter's count tables: the quantity you read is not the value but the *count of a count*, rounded up to a capacity (@sec-cnt-a5).
:::

**14. How do you test a counting solution whose answer you cannot verify by hand?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Three things, all cheap. (1) A brute force at $n \le 9$ with values in a tiny range, fuzzed over hundreds of cases — every pattern in this chapter is locked that way (120 trials for the span credits, 80 for the at-most/exactly pair, 40 for the triplets). (2) A second independent framing, since rungs 2 and 3 disagree informatively: sweep vs $\sum \binom{c}{2}$, prefix-hash vs at-most difference, and they must agree exactly. (3) Structural invariants that fail loudly: credit rows sum to $\binom{n+1}{2}$, cover counts sum to $\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}$, answers are monotone in $K$, and $\text{exactly}(K) \le \text{atMost}(K)$ (@sec-cnt-a1, @sec-cnt-a2, @sec-cnt-a4; the harness is @sec-cnt-why's bookkeeping).
:::

**15. How do you sum $|a_i - a_j|$ over all pairs when $n = 10^5$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sort; the set of pairs does not change. In sorted order $|b_m - b_k| = b_m - b_k$ for $k < m$, so the element of rank $k$ is added $k$ times (as the larger member) and subtracted $n - 1 - k$ times, weight $2k - n + 1$. $O(n \log n)$ for the sort and one pass. The running form `total += k * x - prefix` is the same sum and generalises to any charge linear in the earlier member. Use 64 bits: with $n = 10^5$, half the values at $0$ and half at $10^9$, the answer is $(n/2)^2 \cdot 10^9 = 2.5 \cdot 10^{18}$, which still fits a signed 64-bit integer (@sec-cnt-pairsum, @sec-cnt-psum-weird).
:::

**16. Why is a single histogram wrong for counting pairs with $j - i = a_i + a_j$, and what works instead?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Rewrite as $i + a_i = j - a_j$. The two sides are different functions of the index, so the relation is not "same key" and $\binom{c}{2}$ over one key counts something else. Sweep $j$ left to right: add the number of earlier indices whose left key equals $j - a_j$, then file $j + a_j$. Keys above $n$ can be dropped, so an array of size $n + 1$ replaces the hash map (@sec-cnt-idxval, @sec-cnt-pidx-message).
:::

**17. When does complementary counting need inclusion–exclusion, and how do you get the intersection term?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Whenever the bad set is a union of events that can happen together. Each object in $A \cap B$ is subtracted once for $A$ and once for $B$, so it is added back once: $|U| - |A| - |B| + |A \cap B|$. The intersection is usually either provably empty (distinct couples cannot share both a boy and a girl) or another quantity of the same shape (windows containing neither $x$ nor $y$ are again runs). Say which one it is out loud — that is the step interviewers check (@sec-cnt-comp, @sec-cnt-pcomp-ball).
:::

**18. How do you count increasing triples $i < j < k$, which index do you fix, and can you beat $O(n^2)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Fix the middle: $\sum_j (\#\text{smaller on the left}) \cdot (\#\text{larger on the right})$, exact because nothing relates $a_i$ to $a_k$ directly. Counting both sides by scanning is $O(n^2)$. Both counts are prefix counts over values, so a Fenwick tree over (compressed) values gives each in $O(\log n)$ and the whole answer in $O(n \log n)$; when the values are small, a cumulative table does the same job (@sec-cnt-a5, @sec-cnt-p4-teams).
:::

## Summary

::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"}
- **Contribution swap.** $\sum_{\text{windows}} = \sum_i (\text{charge}_i)$: for a linear statistic the charge is the cover count $(i+1)(n-i)$ (odd length: $\lceil (i+1)(n-i)/2 \rceil$); for an extremal one it is $L_i R_i$, two monotonic-stack spans measured with *opposite* tie-breaks (@sec-cnt-a1, @sec-cnt-a2).
- **Sums over pairs.** Algebra for separable terms; sort and weight rank $k$ by $2k - n + 1$ for distances; per bit $c_b(n - c_b)$ for XOR (@sec-cnt-pairsum).
- **Pairs.** Fix the right end and add `seen[complement]`, or close an equivalence class with $\binom{c}{2}$. Modular conditions key on $t \bmod k$ and look up $(-t) \bmod k$; residues $0$ and $k/2$ self-pair and must not be squared (@sec-cnt-a3, @sec-cnt-p2-songs).
- **Index and value conditions.** Rewrite until each side mentions one index: one key means a histogram, two keys mean a sweep that reads one and writes the other, no separation means a bound and a harmonic enumeration (@sec-cnt-idxval).
- **Windows with a property.** Prefix equality (`ans += cnt[p - K]`, seeded `cnt[0] = 1`) works on any integers; $\text{exactly}(K) = \text{atMost}(K) - \text{atMost}(K-1)$ only on a monotone window statistic; shape properties decompose into runs, $\sum_{\text{runs}} \binom{L+1}{2}$ (@sec-cnt-a4, @sec-cnt-p3-ones).
- **Complement.** $|U|$ minus the bad set; for two overlapping bad events $|U| - |A| - |B| + |A \cap B|$ (@sec-cnt-comp).
- **Triples.** Pivot on the index that appears in two of the three conditions. With no condition between the ends, multiply left and right counts. Otherwise the leftover is one interval $[\max(a_j - a, a_k - c), \min(a_j + a, a_k + c)]$, clamped to $[0, V]$ and answered by a subtraction on a cumulative histogram — $O(nV + n^2)$ (@sec-cnt-a5, @sec-cnt-p4-triplets).
- **Small values.** Let the value be the address: $\mathrm{cnt}[v] = v$ is a table read, and when the interesting quantity is itself a frequency, index the table by it (`how[f]`) and move the cursors lazily (@sec-cnt-p5-lucky, @sec-cnt-p5-beauty).
:::

- One decision generates all eight patterns: *enumerate the object that is fewer*. There are $\binom{n+1}{2}$ windows but $n$ slots; there are $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs but $n$ right ends, $30$ bit columns or $n$ ranks; there are $\binom{n}{3}$ triples but $n$ middle indices. The chapter is that sentence applied eight times, with a different credit each time (@sec-cnt-why).
- Every swap has to be *exact*, and exactness is checked by double counting, not by trusting the derivation: the cover counts sum to $\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}$, a winner-credit row sums to $\binom{n+1}{2}$, and two independent framings of the same condition must agree on hundreds of random cases before you ship either (@sec-cnt-a1, @sec-cnt-a2, @sec-cnt-a4).
- The answer is a number that grows, so decide its type before you decide the algorithm: $\binom{60000}{2} = 1{,}799{,}970{,}000$ is a coin-flip away from $2^{31} - 1$, $\binom{10^5}{2} = 4{,}999{,}950{,}000$ is past it, and the sum of maxima over all windows at $n = 1000$ with values up to $10^9$ is about $5 \cdot 10^{14}$ (@sec-cnt-a3, @sec-arr-size-trap).
- The three framings for "windows with a property" are ordered by what they are allowed to assume — prefix hash (any integers), residue map (any integers, with normalisation in C++/Java), at-most difference (non-negative only). Part of the skill is picking the strongest tool your condition permits, and part of it is knowing that you may not (@sec-cnt-a4, @sec-cnt-p3-binsum).
- "Index condition" and "value condition" are different machinery: positions are handled by the order of your loops (or folded into a per-index key), values by a table indexed by value. Problems that mix them (ABC 166 E, LC 1534, LC 1442) split cleanly once you name which is which (@sec-cnt-idxval, @sec-cnt-a5).
- Complementary counting is the same swap wearing a different hat: count the bad objects because there are fewer *kinds* of them, then subtract from a universe you know in closed form. Every "count the things with property $P$" has a "count the things with $\lnot P$" next to it, the two always add up to the universe, and overlapping bad events cost one inclusion–exclusion term (@sec-cnt-comp, @sec-cnt-pcomp).

## Practice ladder

Ordered by concept, following the eight patterns. The seventeen problems solved in Part B are marked `.solved`; every other entry is "solve it after the lesson named". Counting pairs and triples is what many Codeforces Div. 2 B and C problems are made of, so the Codeforces entries are the ones to do under a timer.

::: {.practice}
- [LC 1588 · Sum of All Odd Length Subarrays](https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-all-odd-length-subarrays/){.solved difficulty="Easy"} — the cover count with one parity filter on it (@sec-cnt-p1-oddsum).
- [LC 2063 · Vowels of All Substrings](https://leetcode.com/problems/vowels-of-all-substrings/){difficulty="Medium"} — the cover count $(i+1)(n-i)$ charged only at vowels; @eq-cnt-swap in one line.
- [CF 608B · Hamming Distance Sum](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/608/B){rating="1500"} — cover counts when the window slides over a *second* string: charge each position of the short string by the alignments that reach it (@sec-cnt-a1).
- [LC 2104 · Sum of Subarray Ranges](https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-subarray-ranges/){.solved difficulty="Medium"} — the same swap when the statistic is extremal: two stack passes, opposite tie-breaks, one subtraction (@sec-cnt-p1-ranges).
- [LC 907 · Sum of Subarray Minimums](https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-subarray-minimums/){difficulty="Medium"} — the min half of 2104 on its own, with the modulus; the stack is developed in the stack volume.
- [LC 2262 · Total Appeal of A String](https://leetcode.com/problems/total-appeal-of-a-string/){difficulty="Hard"} — contribution where a character is charged the windows in which it is the *first* occurrence of its letter.
- [LC 477 · Total Hamming Distance](https://leetcode.com/problems/total-hamming-distance/){.solved difficulty="Medium"} — one bit column at a time, $c(n-c)$ (@sec-cnt-psum-hamming).
- [CF 1420B · Rock and Lever](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1420/B){rating="1200"} — $a_i \,\&\, a_j \ge a_i \oplus a_j$ means "same highest bit"; group by it and add $\binom{c}{2}$.
- [CF 1648A · Weird Sum](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1648/A){.solved rating="1400"} — group, split coordinates, sort, weight by rank (@sec-cnt-psum-weird).
- [LC 1685 · Sum of Absolute Differences in a Sorted Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-absolute-differences-in-a-sorted-array/){difficulty="Medium"} — the rank weight per element, with prefix sums (@sec-cnt-pairsum).
- [CF 1311F · Moving Points](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1311/F){rating="1900"} — pairwise distances over the pairs that never meet; counts and sums of earlier points by speed need a Fenwick tree.
- [LC 1512 · Number of Good Pairs](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-good-pairs/){.solved difficulty="Easy"} — sweep and histogram, both, in the same write-up (@sec-cnt-p2-goodpairs).
- [LC 1128 · Number of Equivalent Domino Pairs](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-equivalent-domino-pairs/){difficulty="Easy"} — equivalence under reversal plus a normalised key; exercise 16.
- [CF 50B · Choosing Symbol Pairs](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/50/B){rating="1500"} — a pair count over a character histogram, where ordered versus unordered is the entire problem (@sec-cnt-a3).
- [LC 1010 · Pairs of Songs With Total Durations Divisible by 60](https://leetcode.com/problems/pairs-of-songs-with-total-durations-divisible-by-60/){.solved difficulty="Medium"} — complementary residues with two self-pairing classes (@sec-cnt-p2-songs).
- [AC abc166_e · This Message Will Self-Destruct in 5s](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc166/tasks/abc166_e){.solved} — two keys, one sweep (@sec-cnt-pidx-message).

- [LC 2475 · Number of Unequal Triplets in Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-unequal-triplets-in-array/){.solved difficulty="Easy"} — $\binom{n}{3}$ minus the triples that repeat a value (@sec-cnt-pcomp-unequal).

- [LC 1395 · Count Number of Teams](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-number-of-teams/){.solved difficulty="Medium"} — fix the middle, multiply the sides (@sec-cnt-p4-teams).

## Further reading

- [Wikipedia — Tetrahedral number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahedral_number) — $\sum_i (i+1)(n-i) = \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6} = \binom{n+2}{3}$, the total of the cover counts in @sec-cnt-a1.
- [Wikipedia — Binomial coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_coefficient) — the identities behind $\binom{n+1}{2}$ windows, $\binom{L+1}{2}$ windows per run, and the hockey-stick sum $\sum_k \binom{k}{2} = \binom{n+1}{3}$.
- [CP-Algorithms — The Inclusion-Exclusion Principle](https://cp-algorithms.com/combinatorics/inclusion-exclusion.html) — complementary counting and inclusion–exclusion over many events, with contest applications (@sec-cnt-comp).
- [CP-Algorithms — Fenwick tree](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/fenwick.html) — the structure that turns "how many earlier values are smaller?" into $O(\log n)$, the missing piece for inversions and for increasing triples at large $n$ (@sec-cnt-a3, @sec-cnt-p4-teams).
- [USACO Guide — Introduction to Prefix Sums](https://usaco.guide/silver/prefix-sums) — prefix sums with the CSES counting problems *Subarray Sums II* (prefix equality with a map) and *Subarray Divisibility* (equal residues), the two framings of @sec-cnt-a4.
- [Wikipedia — Double counting (proof technique)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_counting_(proof_technique)) — counting one set in two ways, the argument behind the swap of summation order in @eq-cnt-swap and every credit check in this chapter.
